node.name: The one truth (ekaṃ sat)
node.principle: ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti — "Truth is one; the wise call it by many names." (Ṛgveda 1.164.46)
node.status: working hypothesis of this ontology (the user's first principle), not a claim any single tradition makes about all the others
node.how_to_read: Each item in `views` records how one lineage names and describes what it takes to be ultimate (or why it posits none), in that lineage's own terms and with the text-layer teachings it rests on. The claim that these are views of one truth is made only here, in the interpretation layer, and always together with each tradition's own objections (the `caveat` and `tradition_denies_single_ultimate` fields). Traditions that reject a single ultimate — e.g. Madhyamaka (no ultimate entity), Theravāda (nibbāna is not a ground or a self), Dvaita (eternal difference), Nyāya and Jainism (many selves), Mīmāṃsā and Cārvāka (no such ultimate) — are recorded as rejecting it, not silently absorbed.

descriptions: The self shining by self-experience, whose nature is consciousness, cutting through all other states (Samayasāra-kalaśa 1).
One, pure, made of perception and knowledge, formless; not even an atom of anything else is mine (Samayasāra 38).
Who the supreme self is, that am I (Yogīndu, Yogasāra 22).
negations: Not the body, not karma, not the passions (Iṣṭopadeśa 50).
Not the doer of material karma in the ultimate standpoint.
views.relation_to_self: Identical with one's own pure self as seen by the ultimate standpoint; realised through discriminative knowledge and self-experience.
views.relation_to_world: The world of substances is real; the self is its knower, not its maker; conventional conduct belongs to the path, not to the self's nature.
views.caveat: 'I am the supreme self' in the Adhyātma texts means that each soul's own nature is the perfected state, not that all souls are one Brahman; the movement accepts the Jain plurality of souls and the reality of the world, and its mature form insists on holding the conventional standpoint alongside the ultimate.

names.name: Sākṣin (as witness of the three states)
Īśvara (Brahman as associated with māyā, empirical level)

descriptions: existence, consciousness, infinitude — satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma (TU 2.1.1) as its own-nature definition (svarūpa-lakṣaṇa)
being–consciousness–bliss (sat-cit-ānanda)
one without a second (ekam evādvitīyam, ChU 6.2.1)
self-luminous (svaprakāśa), never an object
the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) of the world-appearance, as the rope is of the snake
the world's cause, defined incidentally (taṭastha-lakṣaṇa) as that from which the world arises (BS 1.1.2)
negations: neti neti — not so, not so (BĀU 2.3.6; BS 3.2.22)
no dissolution, no origination, none bound, no seeker, no liberated — this is the highest truth (GK 2.32)
without parts, attributes, action or difference of any of the three kinds (sajātīya, vijātīya, svagata)
views.relation_to_self: Identical: the inner self (pratyag-ātman) of every being is Brahman (tat tvam asi; ahaṃ brahmāsmi). The jīva is Brahman appearing as limited or reflected through adjuncts produced by ignorance.
views.relation_to_world: The world is superimposed on Brahman and is its apparent transformation (vivarta); Brahman is its material and efficient cause through māyā. The world is real for empirical purposes (vyāvahārika) until knowledge, then sublated; ultimately it is not other than Brahman.
views.caveat: Advaita accepts that truth is one (and reads RV 1.164.46 in that sense), but the one is non-dual consciousness without any internal difference: the personal Lord is Brahman as associated with māyā, real at the empirical level only. Advaita would reject any 'one-truth' reading that makes the world, or plural selves, or a personal God ultimately real, and rejects equating its Brahman with a sum or organism of parts.

descriptions: Śiva present equally in what is pure and impure, feared and loved
the state beyond the eight fetters, in which the bound paśu becomes Maheśvara (Kulārṇava 13.91)
views.relation_to_self: The one freed from the fetters is himself Maheśvara; the guru is Śiva.
views.relation_to_world: The world, including the cremation ground and what is loathed, is not other than Śiva.
views.caveat: Aghora's own texts (Kīnārām's Vivekasār etc.) are not yet extracted; this view rests on the shared Kaula doctrine of the fetters and on the lineage's self-description, and should be revised from its own writings.

names.name: the end of suffering after the fixed round (dukkhass' anta)

descriptions: (As reported) All beings are transformed by niyati, saṅgati and bhāva (DN 2).
(As reported) Pleasure and pain are measured out as with a measure; saṃsāra has fixed limits (DN 2).
(Tamil report) The lord is the boundless knower who pervades endless things everywhere and always; release is reached in the supreme white birth (Maṇimēkalai 27.108–165).
negations: No cause or condition for the defilement or purification of beings (DN 2).
No exertion, strength, energy or human effort (Uvāsagadasāo 7).
views.relation_to_self: (As reported) The jīva is real and transmigrates through the fixed round; in the Jain account a soul can re-enter successive bodies (reanimation).
views.relation_to_world: (As reported) The world-course is fixed in every detail and runs through 8,400,000 great aeons for every being.
views.caveat: No Ājīvika text survives; every statement comes from hostile Buddhist, Jain or Tamil sources. Niyati is a governing order, not a ground of being, and the sources never present it as 'the one truth'. The Tamil report of a 'lord who is the boundless knower' may refer to the omniscient teacher rather than a creator; it is recorded as the source gives it.

descriptions: (As reported) To every question about the other world, spontaneously born beings, fruit of deeds and the Tathāgata after death, in all four forms, the answer is refused (DN 2).
negations: 'I do not say it is so, nor thus, nor otherwise, nor not so, nor not not so.'
views.relation_to_self: Not asserted: (Jain report) 'who knows whether the soul exists, and what use is knowing it?'
views.relation_to_world: Not asserted.
views.caveat: The Ajñānikas refuse to affirm any ultimate; to read their refusal as pointing to an ineffable one truth would be an interpretation they are reported to reject as another assertion. Both Buddhist and Jain reporters insist their own undeclared points and 'inexpressible' (avaktavya) differ from this refusal.

names.name: rasa (relish) — as the 'twin' of tasting Brahman
brahmāsvāda-sahodara (twin of the taste of Brahman)

descriptions: arising from the predominance of sattva, undivided, self-luminous, made of bliss and consciousness, untouched by any other object, the twin of tasting Brahman, whose life is supermundane wonder (SD 3.2–3)
for Abhinavagupta: the relish of one's own consciousness, universalized and at rest (viśrānti)
negations: not identical with tasting Brahman: it depends on determinants and lasts while the work is enjoyed (implied in 'sahodara')
views.relation_to_self: In rasa the spectator relishes his own consciousness freed from personal limitation (Abhinavagupta); in śānta the stable emotion is knowledge of the self (tattvajñāna).
views.relation_to_world: Drama imitates the moods of the three worlds (NŚ 1.107); rasa is 'supermundane' (alaukika), neither real nor unreal in the ordinary sense.
views.caveat: Poetics is not a darśana and does not itself posit an ultimate. It compares aesthetic relish with realization, explicitly as a 'twin', not an identity; each author supplies the ultimate from his own school (Abhinavagupta: Trika Śaivism; Viśvanātha: Vedānta; Rūpa Gosvāmī: Kṛṣṇa). Advaita treats the relish of bliss in samādhi (rasāsvāda) as an obstacle (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 3.45), a contrast to be kept.

names.name: Perumāḷ / Emperumāṉ (the Great One / our Lord)
Tiruvaraṅkaṉ, Tiruvēṅkaṭamuṭaiyāṉ and the other names of the Lord at each sung site

descriptions: He who has the highest good, beyond which there is nothing higher; lord of the unwearying immortals; whose radiant feet end sorrow (TVM 1.1.1).
When there was no god, no world and no life, he created the four-faced Brahmā with the gods, worlds and lives (TVM 4.10.1); Nārāyaṇa made Brahmā and Brahmā made Śaṅkara (Nāṉmukaṉ Tiruvantāti 1).
He pervades all things hidden within them as life within a body (TVM 1.1.7).
Easy of access to those who love him, hard to reach for others (TVM 1.3.1); he takes whatever form and name his devotees delight in (Mutal Tiruvantāti 44).
He dwells with Śrī on his chest, who says she cannot part from him even for a moment (TVM 6.10.10).
He is present in the temple image at Śrīraṅgam, Tiruvēṅkaṭam and the other sung sites, awakened at dawn, praised with benedictions for his own safety (Tiruppallāṇṭu; Tiruppaḷḷiyeḻucci).
negations: Not one god among many: the Āḻvārs repeatedly deny that the other gods are refuges (Nāṉmukaṉ Tiruvantāti; Madhurakavi's 'I know no other god' is said of his teacher).
views.relation_to_self: The self belongs to the Lord as servant to master: 'I thought I was my own and what I had was mine; I am yours and what I have is yours' (TVM 2.9.9); its fulfilment is faultless service at all times (TVM 3.3.1).
views.relation_to_world: The world and lives are his creation and his body; he is hidden in them as life in a body (TVM 1.1.7) and swallowed and restored them (the 'world-swallower' image); the world is real and is the field of his play and avatāras.
views.caveat: The Āḻvārs and the Śrīvaiṣṇava commentators would reject any one-truth reading that makes Nārāyaṇa one name among equals for an impersonal absolute or that treats Śiva, Brahmā or other gods as independent refuges; the Lord is one, but he is Nārāyaṇa with Śrī, personal and qualified.

descriptions: There is only One; all forms of God and all paths are that One.
views.relation_to_self: Self-realization is realizing that One as one's own Self.
views.relation_to_world: Everything that happens is God's play; nothing is apart from the One.
views.caveat: Devotees hold Anandamayi Ma herself to be a manifestation of the Divine; the one-truth reading fits her teaching but not every devotee's view of her person.

descriptions: Śiva worshipped exclusively in the liṅga, with Vedic rites retained
views.relation_to_self: Not recorded in this skeleton.
views.relation_to_world: Not recorded in this skeleton.
views.caveat: Skeleton only; the Ārādhya view needs sourcing from Telugu texts.

descriptions: the fourth empty, clear light (Pañcakrama 2.4–5)
the union where saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the two truths, grasped and grasper become one (Pañcakrama 5.2–13)
non-dual gnosis, non-abiding nirvāṇa, buddhahood (Pañcakrama 5.25)
negations: 'unborn' and other such words only point to non-dual gnosis (Pañcakrama 5.27)
views.relation_to_self: The self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna) body is the conventional truth, the illusory body of the yogin himself.
views.relation_to_world: The world is not self-arisen; its cause is clear light (Pañcakrama 3.15).
views.caveat: Clear light is 'all-empty' and non-dual gnosis — the tradition frames it within the two truths of Madhyamaka and would not accept it as a self-existent absolute.

descriptions: the Lord (pati) as the one independent cause, acting by his own will
the Lord's knowledge and action are unsurpassed; liberation brings the soul into his proximity and union, sharing his powers (Pāśupata)
for the skull-observers the Lord is Kapālin/Bhairava, whose penance they re-enact
negations: the Lord is not dependent on karma (PABh on PS 2.6)
views.relation_to_self: Souls are eternal paśus distinct from the Lord; liberation is the end of their suffering by the Lord's grace.
views.relation_to_world: The Lord emits and withdraws the effects (the world and the embodied souls) at will; he is their cause.
views.caveat: The Atimārga schools are theistic and keep the liberated soul distinct from the Lord; they would reject a reading that dissolves the soul into an impersonal absolute. The Mantramārga ranks their goal below its own (Svacchanda 11.71). For the Lākula, Kāpālika and Kālāmukha divisions almost no first-hand doctrinal text survives.

names.name: the unmanifest (avyakta), knower of the field

descriptions: The supreme self is changeless, eternal, the seer, cause of consciousness together with mind, the elements' qualities and the senses (Ca Sū 1.56).
Disengagement is release: the supreme, tranquil, imperishable — that is brahman, that is liberation (Ca Śā 5.11); sinless, passionless, deathless, brahman, nirvāṇa (5.23).
The person is the measure of the world: brahman is the inner self (Śā 5.4-5).
negations: The self become brahman is not perceived and has no mark (Ca Śā 1.155).
'This is not I, this is not mine' (Ca Śā 1.153).
views.relation_to_self: The individual self is eternal, beginningless and (for Caraka) all-pervading; the empirical person is the aggregate born of delusion, desire, aversion and karma; release is that self 'become brahman'.
views.relation_to_world: The world is real and made of the five elements; the person and the world correspond member for member; seeing oneself in all and all in oneself gives rise to the true understanding.
views.caveat: Āyurveda is a science of life rather than a soteriology: its purpose is health (Ca Sū 30.26), and its metaphysics (chiefly Caraka Śā 1 and 5, Suśruta Śā 1) is close to Sāṃkhya-Yoga and Vaiśeṣika. No creator is required — Kāṅkāyana's Prajāpati-theory is rejected in Ca Sū 25, and Suśruta leaves the 'source' open among nature, the Lord, time, chance, destiny and transformation (Su Śā 1.11); Caraka and Suśruta differ on whether selves are all-pervading. It would reject any reading that makes medicine itself the means of liberation, while holding health to be the root of all four aims.

names.name: Amitābha and the Western Land, read through the Tiantai 'four lands'

descriptions: Mao Ziyuan taught the 'perfect interfusion of the four lands and three contemplations' (Lushan lianzong baojian).
views.relation_to_self: The lay practitioner keeps the five precepts and recites to purify the five roots.
views.relation_to_world: The five turbidities of this world are to be left through the five precepts and recitation.
views.caveat: Known only through its defender Pudu's compilation; views of the later White Lotus sects are not represented here.

descriptions: the founder as God
negations: not the brahmanical gods
views.relation_to_self: Devotion to the founder.
views.relation_to_world: Caste religion rejected.
views.caveat: Low-confidence characterization from ethnographic reports.

descriptions: When no thought arises, that itself is seeing the Buddha; no-thought includes precepts, samādhi and wisdom (Lidai fabao ji).
negations: Thought arising is like the back of a mirror, which reflects nothing (Lidai fabao ji, Musang's saying).
views.caveat: Baotang's own record; Zongmi reported it as rejecting all practice. Moderate-low confidence in the formulation.

descriptions: Two distinct eternal entities: Parabrahman the supreme, and Akṣarabrahman his ideal devotee and abode, manifest in the guru.
views.relation_to_self: The liberated soul becomes brahmarūpa (like Akṣara) and eternally serves Parabrahman.
views.relation_to_world: The world is real, created by Parabrahman through Akṣara and māyā.
views.caveat: The Ahmedabad and Vadtal dioceses reject the identification of Akṣara with Guṇātītānanda and his successors; see dsp:akshar-purushottam.

names.name: the Man of the Heart (maner mānuṣ)

descriptions: dwells in this human body
near yet a hundred thousand leagues away
seen through the guru
worship of the human makes one golden
negations: not in temple or mosque
not in scripture (anumān)
without caste
views.relation_to_self: The Man lives in one's own body, neighbour in the mirror-city, unseen until the guru reveals him.
views.relation_to_world: What is in the body is in the universe; the world outside is known through the body.
views.caveat: The Bāuls refuse the scriptural names and doctrinal frames (Vedāntic, Vaiṣṇava or Islamic) in which the 'one truth' might be stated; the ultimate is the living human, verifiable in the body.

descriptions: Kāmākhyā is dharma, artha, kāma and liberation; nothing in the three worlds exists without her (Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.9-13)
the subtle root-nature (mūla-prakṛti) who divided herself into māyā and vidyā to bring about creation (Bṛhaddharma Purāṇa madhya 6.98-124)
the Mother (Mā) of the devotional songs, both terrible and tender
negations: herself without the three guṇas, she shines through the one who has them (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.120)
views.relation_to_self: The devotee is her child; the digests adopt the Kaula and Vedāntic teaching that the self is one with the Goddess.
views.relation_to_world: The earth bears her body in the pīṭhas, where the parts of Satī fell (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.40-50).
views.caveat: Devotional Bengal Śāktism keeps the relation of child and Mother and resists merging it into an impersonal absolute; ritual texts of the same region keep sharp distinctions of eligibility (caste, bhāva) that a one-truth reading should not erase.

descriptions: Vāsudeva the Lord is the knower of the field, whose self is without guṇas (MBh 12.326.38)
the fourfold form (caturmūrti): Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha (12.326.68–69, 12.326.93)
the dwelling of all (sarvāvāsa), the supreme self entered by the liberated (12.332.17)
the culmination (niṣṭhā) of every system of knowledge (12.337.63–64)
the one who appears again and again to protect the worlds (12.326.71–94)
negations: without guṇas (nirguṇātmaka) (12.326.38; 12.332.17)
not seen by those without one-pointed devotion; even Brahmā has not had such a sight (12.326.96)
views.relation_to_self: The individual self is Saṃkarṣaṇa, arising from Vāsudeva (12.326.38, 12.326.68); the liberated enter Vāsudeva through the sun and the vyūhas, the ekāntins directly (12.332.13–18; 12.336.3).
views.relation_to_world: From Aniruddha comes Brahmā, from Brahmā all moving and unmoving beings, at the beginning of each kalpa (12.326.69–70); the Lord withdraws the world at the end of a thousand ages and dwells alone with knowledge (12.326.66–67).
views.caveat: Described both as the Lord with a form and as without guṇas; the later schools that inherit this devotion (Pāñcarātra, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, Gauḍīya) reject an impersonal reading of it, while Advaita readers take the personal Lord as Brahman with attributes. The Nārāyaṇīya itself records the Pāśupata system as a distinct knowledge (12.337.59, 62) and states that Rudra and Nārāyaṇa are one being made twofold (12.328.24).

names.name: Hari, Kṛṣṇa (as the object of the gopīs' love, NBS 21)

descriptions: The Lord who, when sung of, quickly manifests himself and makes his devotees experience him (NBS 80).
The Lord dislikes pride and loves humility (NBS 27).
Love for him (prema) is indescribable, like a mute's tasting; free of the guṇas and of desire, increasing every moment, unbroken, subtlest, of the nature of experience (NBS 51–54).
Three views of the object of devotion: the Lord's majesty as other (Kāśyapa), the one self (Bādarāyaṇa), both (Śāṇḍilya) (ŚBS, as recalled).
views.relation_to_self: Devotees are 'His own' (tadīya, NBS 73); there is no difference between the Lord and his people (NBS 41). ŚBS: Śāṇḍilya holds devotion bears on both the Lord as other and the self as one (low confidence on the exact sūtras).
views.relation_to_world: Worldly and Vedic activity is to be laid down in him (nirodha, NBS 8); until love is attained worldly activity is not abandoned but its fruit is given up (NBS 62).
views.caveat: The bhakti-śāstra would reject a one-truth reading that makes devotion a preparatory stage to be surpassed by impersonal knowledge: for the Nārada Sūtra love is the fruit itself (NBS 26, 30).

descriptions: immeasurable bliss and knowledge, deathless, whose apparent transformations the elements are, through two indescribable ignorances (Bhāmatī, opening verse)
negations: as in Advaita generally
views.relation_to_self: The jīva is Brahman as delimited (avacchinna) by the inner organ; ignorance resides in the jīvas, not in pure Brahman.
views.relation_to_world: The world is Brahman's apparent transformation (vivarta) through the avidyās of the jīvas, with Brahman as its object.
views.caveat: Shares Advaita's ultimate; differs only in the theory of the locus of ignorance and of the jīva. Partisans hold this theory to be correct.

names.name: the self in its own nature after release

descriptions: Kumārila opens the Ślokavārttika by saluting the one whose body is pure knowledge, whose divine eye is the three Vedas, the cause of attaining the good, the bearer of the half-moon (ŚV pratijñā 1).
Liberation is the absolute dissolution of the self's threefold bond — body, senses and objects (Śāstradīpikā on MS 1.1.5).

Dharma performed with its declared aim produces that aim; performed with the thought of offering it to Govinda / Īśvara it becomes a cause of the highest good (Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa, Arthasaṅgraha, conclusions).
negations: No creator Prajāpati and no total dissolution (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 42–116).
Liberation is not an enjoyment of pleasure, which would be only another name for a perishable heaven (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 105).
views.relation_to_self: Each self is eternal and all-pervading; release leaves it in its own nature, without body, senses or objects (for Pārthasārathi, without bliss; for other Bhāṭṭas he reports, with innate bliss).
views.relation_to_world: The world is real; creation and dissolution are to be understood 'as today', i.e. as the ongoing births and deaths of beings, not as a total destruction and re-creation (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 113).
views.caveat: The Bhāṭṭa school does not posit one ultimate reality; its ontology is pluralist and realist. The salutation to the moon-crested one in ŚV pratijñā 1 and the late dedication of dharma to Govinda/Īśvara (Āpadeva, Laugākṣi Bhāskara) show devotion, not a doctrine that the Lord is the one ground of being. Advaitins adopt Bhāṭṭa epistemology for empirical matters only, and Bhāṭṭas do not accept the Advaitic reading of their system.

descriptions: Brahman is one as cause and many as effect; the world and souls are its real transformations (pariṇāma) through its power (śakti).
Bhāskara: difference from the soul is due to real adjuncts (upādhi), non-difference is natural.
Yādavaprakāśa: Brahman is naturally both one and many, transforming into Īśvara, the souls and matter.
Vijñānabhikṣu: souls and prakṛti are non-separate (avibhāga) from Brahman, which is their substrate.
negations: Denies that the world is an illusory appearance (vivarta) of Brahman.
Denies that difference is merely imagined through a positive avidyā.
views.relation_to_self: The soul is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman, limited by real adjuncts (Bhāskara) or naturally distinct-yet-one (Yādava); at liberation, after death, it becomes non-different from Brahman.
views.relation_to_world: The world is Brahman's real effect and is non-different from it as cause; it is neither false nor wholly other.
views.caveat: The school would reject a one-truth reading that treats its difference as merely provisional; for Bhāskara the adjuncts that make the difference are real until death.

descriptions: Consciousness (Śiva) and energy (Śakti) unite when kuṇḍalinī reaches sahasrāra.
views.relation_to_self: The awakened consciousness is one's own Self.
views.relation_to_world: The world is manifest energy (Śakti).
views.caveat: The school presents much of its teaching as practical method; its metaphysics follows tantra and Vedānta without a single fixed doctrine.

names.name: Kuntu Zangpo, the primordial buddha of Bön
bon nyid (the reality of Bön) and bon sku (the Bön-body)

descriptions: The base (kun gzhi) is empty and clear, and awareness (rig pa) is inseparable from it; their union is called 'mother and son' (ma bu) in the Zhang Zhung Nyengyü (moderate confidence).
Kuntu Zangpo is the Bön-body; Shenlha Ökar the body of perfection; Tönpa Shenrab the emanation body.
negations: the base is not a thing established by characteristics; awareness cannot be grasped as an object
views.relation_to_self: The nature of one's own mind (sems nyid) is the base; recognizing it is Buddhahood.
views.relation_to_world: Appearances arise from the base as light, sound and rays; not recognizing them as the base's own display is the origin of saṃsāra.
views.caveat: Bön insists on its own origin (Tönpa Shenrab, Tagzig) and would reject being read as a variant of Buddhism; its 'kun gzhi' is the ultimate base, whereas in Nyingma usage 'kun gzhi' (all-base) usually names the ground of saṃsāric consciousness — the same word is not the same doctrine.
views.notes: Optional (Bön). Built from general knowledge; confidence low-moderate.

descriptions: the goal of the sequential installation of meditative qualities in the body, reached through the path and fruit
views.caveat: Very little of the tradition's own discursive statements on the ultimate is available; entry minimal and low confidence.

descriptions: The Supreme Soul is an incorporeal point of light, the Ocean of knowledge, peace and love; he is not omnipresent.
views.relation_to_self: Souls are eternal points of light, distinct from the Supreme Soul; they are his children.
views.relation_to_world: The world drama is real and repeats every 5,000 years.
views.caveat: Explicitly denies God's omnipresence and the identity of soul and God; rejects the Advaita reading.

descriptions: the union of Heruka (means, bliss) and Vajravārāhī (wisdom, emptiness)
the supreme bliss (śrīcakrasaṃvara) that is the 'binding' of the wheel of all phenomena
views.relation_to_self: The yogin's body is the maṇḍala: the twenty-four sites are its channels and the deities reside in it (body maṇḍala).
views.relation_to_world: The land of India (the pīṭhas) is the outer maṇḍala; worlds and bodies correspond.
views.caveat: The etymology 'saṃvara = supreme bliss' is the commentators'; the tradition keeps Heruka empty of own-being and distinguishes him from Śaiva Bhairava, whom he is said to have subdued.

descriptions: 'The numinous source shines bright and pure; the branch streams flow in the dark' (Cantongqi).
The real and the apparent interpenetrate in five ranks (Dongshan).
negations: 'Holding to phenomena is delusion; merging with principle is not yet awakening' (Cantongqi).
views.relation_to_self: 'You are not it; it is just you' (Baojing sanmei).
views.relation_to_world: Principle and phenomena interfuse and yet each abides in its place (huihu / bu huihu).
views.caveat: Caodong's 'real' is not a separate substance: 'it' and 'you' are neither identical nor two.

names.name: the four elements (bhūta-catuṣṭaya) as the only principles
the world as far as the senses reach (yāvān indriyagocaraḥ)

descriptions: (As reported) 'Earth, water, fire, air: these are the principles' (Bṛhaspati Sūtra fragment).
(As reported) The variety of the world — fire hot, water cold, wind temperate — is fixed by svabhāva, not by an unseen cause (Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha 1).
negations: No other world, no self that goes to it (paralokino 'bhāvāt paralokābhāvaḥ).
No heaven or liberation other than pleasure and the death of the body; no lord but the king.
(Jayarāśi) Not even the elements 'stand when examined' — no principle is established.
views.relation_to_self: (As reported) The self is the living body qualified by consciousness; it ends with the body.
views.relation_to_world: (As reported) The world is the perceptible aggregate of four elements.
views.caveat: The Cārvāka denies any ultimate beyond what perception shows and explicitly denies another world, an unseen cause and liberation; Jayarāśi denies that any principle can be established. Any one-truth reading runs against these denials; the school would call it the priests' 'livelihood'.

names.name: original face (benlai mianmu 本來面目)

descriptions: Originally pure, originally unborn and undying, originally complete, originally unmoving, able to produce all dharmas (Huineng's words on awakening, Platform Sūtra 4.13).
The one mind of buddhas and beings, without beginning, neither arisen nor ceased, without form, beyond all measure and names (Huangbo, Chuanxin fayao).
Samādhi is its substance and prajñā its function, like lamp and light (Platform Sūtra 7.1).
negations: 'Originally there is not a single thing' (Platform Sūtra 4.11).
'Neither mind nor buddha' (Mazu).
'Neither cold nor hot, neither blue nor yellow, not belonging to existence or non-existence' (Huangbo).
views.relation_to_self: Not something other than one's own mind: 'if deluded, the buddha is a sentient being; if awakened, the sentient being is a buddha' (Dunhuang Platform Sūtra 52.2).
views.relation_to_world: All dharmas are not apart from the self-nature and are produced by it; mountains, rivers and ordinary activity are its function; the Pure Land is the purified mind.
views.caveat: Chan does not posit an ultimate as an object or a being; names such as buddha-nature and mind are 'expedient names' to be dropped ('if you meet the Buddha, kill the Buddha'). The tradition would reject reading its buddha-nature as a Vedāntic self; Chan critics of the 'Śreṇika heresy' (Nanyang Huizhong) explicitly reject an eternal mind-nature that leaves the body.

descriptions: both the nirguṇa and Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa
views.relation_to_self: The guru is above Hari (Sahajobāī).
views.relation_to_world: Created by Hari; transcended through the guru.
views.caveat: The sampradāya holds nirguṇa and saguṇa together; it would reject a purely impersonal reading.

names.name: the Great Mother, Prajñāpāramitā (yum chen mo)
the meaning of the perfection of wisdom (shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa)
Mahāmudrā, the natural state of mind (phyag rgya chen po)

descriptions: the unborn, empty nature of mind in which ego-clinging has been cut
the natural state resting without fixation once the four māras are cut
negations: gods and demons (lha 'dre) have no existence apart from the mind
the self that is clung to has no root
views.relation_to_self: The self to be cut is ego-clinging (bdag 'dzin); when it is cut, the māras are cut; the Great Mother is the nature of one's own mind.
views.relation_to_world: Appearances, including terrifying ones, are the display of mind; offered without attachment they become the means of cutting clinging.
views.caveat: Chöd presents itself as the practice of the Perfection of Wisdom, not as a separate philosophical system; practitioners explain the ultimate according to their own school (rangtong, shentong, Mahāmudrā or Dzogchen). The Great Mother is both the personified deity and emptiness itself.

names.name: Alakh / Allāh (as the one Lord of Hindu and Turk)

descriptions: the stainless one saluted first in the Vāṇī
met in the unseen
Brahman one without a second (Sundardās)
negations: neither Hindu nor Turk
not in temple or mosque
views.relation_to_self: The Lord is within the body, which is the true mosque and temple; the self erased, Hari remains.
views.relation_to_world: One Lord of all beings; hence no enmity toward any.
views.caveat: Sundardās's Advaita and Dādū's devotional voice coexist; the panth would reject a reading that erases devotion to the guru and the Name.

descriptions: the Dhammakāya, a luminous Buddha-form, is found within at the body's centre
nibbāna described as a true self (attā) and as a realm (āyatana) where the Buddhas abide (the tradition's teaching)
views.relation_to_self: teaches a true self in nibbāna, distinct from the non-self aggregates
views.relation_to_world: the refined inner bodies lead beyond the world
views.caveat: Mainstream Thai Theravāda scholars (notably P. A. Payutto) reject the teaching that nibbāna is a self; recorded as a dispute (dsp:nibbana-atta-or-anatta).

descriptions: Lord of Satlok who sent Kabīr and established Dharamdās's line
negations: not Kāl Nirañjan
views.relation_to_self: The soul is freed by the Name received from the vaṃś ācārya.
views.relation_to_world: The three worlds are Kāl's.
views.caveat: As for the Kabīr Panth generally; the hereditary line is itself part of the soteriology.

descriptions: The liberation of the Buddhas and of the disciples is one, though their paths differ (Vasumitra).
views.relation_to_self: No self (general Sthavira position; no separate record).
views.relation_to_world: Not separately recorded.
views.caveat: Doctrine known only from a few doxographic tenets; this view is a thin reconstruction.

descriptions: The ruler of all, subtler than the subtle, bright as gold, graspable by a mind as if in sleep (MDh 12.122).
Some call him Agni, others Manu, Prajāpati, Indra, the breath, the eternal Brahman (MDh 12.123).
He pervades all beings with the five elements and turns them like a wheel through birth, growth and decay (MDh 12.124).
The self is one and yet many, like space in pots or the sun reflected in many waters (YS 3.144).
All living beings are the city of the one who lies in the cave, unslain and stainless (ĀpDh 1.8.22).
views.relation_to_self: Seeing the self by yoga is the highest dharma (YS 1.8); knowledge of the self is the highest of all means (MDh 12.85); the self is its own witness (MDh 8.84); seeing the self in all beings one reaches Brahman (MDh 12.125).
views.relation_to_world: The world issues from the self-existent (MDh 1.5–6) and revolves through ages and Manu-periods (MDh 1.68–80); dharma differs by age.
views.caveat: Dharmaśāstra itself states the many-names principle (MDh 12.123) but insists that knowledge of the one does not dissolve the duties of class and life-stage before liberation — the debts must be paid first (MDh 6.35–37) — and the 'one-order' teachers subordinate renunciation and liberation to the householder's dharma.

evidence: text:sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/gretil_devanAgarI/1_sanskr/6_sastra/4_dharma/smrti/manu-smrti_plain_text.md (GRETIL, Kullūka vulgate numbering; M = Medhātithi numbering)
checks.note: All the descriptions were found. MDh 12.122–124 (the ruler of all, subtler than the subtle; called Agni, Manu, Prajāpati, Indra, breath, eternal Brahman; turning beings like a wheel), YS 3.144 (one self like the sun in many waters), MDh 12.83–85, YS 1.8 and MDh 6.35–37 are cited in confirmed teaching checks. ĀpDh 1.8.22 (all beings the city of the one in the cave) is also confirmed, with the locator widened to 1.8.22.1–8.

descriptions: from the standpoint of ultimate reality the self is unbound, untouched, not other, constant, undifferentiated and unconjoined (Samayasāra 14)
one, pure, made of perception and knowledge, formless; not an atom of anything else is mine (Samayasāra 38)
the knowing state beyond all stages of quality (Samayasāra 6)
free of the eighteen faults, including hunger and thirst (Niyamasāra 6)
negations: in truth there is no knowledge, conduct or faith as separate attributes of the knower (Samayasāra 7)
not reached in a clothed or female body
not a creator
views.relation_to_self: The pure self is the soul's own nature now, seen from the ultimate standpoint; the conventional standpoint describes the bound soul in order to lead it there.
views.relation_to_world: Real and uncreated; karmic matter and the soul occasion each other's changes without either becoming the other.
views.caveat: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator: liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct, and the universe of six substances is uncreated. It can accept 'one truth, many names' only in its own way — as many-sidedness (anekānta) about a plural reality — not as the identity of all souls in one substance. Kundakunda's language of the pure self is sometimes compared with Advaita; the Digambara tradition insists the pure self is each individual soul's own, not a universal Brahman.

descriptions: Brahman as existence-consciousness-bliss, reached by the synthesis of all yogas.
views.relation_to_self: The Self is Brahman (Advaita).
views.relation_to_world: The world is māyā from the standpoint of the ultimate; to be served as God in practice.
views.caveat: DLS also worships personal deities and teaches devotion; its Advaita is practised within a synthesis.

names.name: the single intent (dgongs gcig) of the Buddha's word

descriptions: The whole of the Buddha's teaching has one intent, whose heart is Mahāmudrā; realized through the fivefold practice (bodhicitta, deity, guru, view, dedication).
negations: not reached by view alone without bodhicitta and devotion (the fivefold teaching)
views.relation_to_self: As in the Kagyu generally: the mind's own nature.
views.relation_to_world: The vows and practices of all vehicles are aspects of one intent rather than rival systems.
views.caveat: 'Single intent' concerns the unity of the Buddha's teaching, not a metaphysical monism.

names.name: Mahāmudrā, co-emergent union (lhan cig skyes sbyor)

descriptions: The co-emergent: mind-as-such is dharmakāya, appearances its light, thoughts its waves; adversity, illness and death, carried onto the path, are of one taste with it (the six equal tastes).
negations: not found by rejecting thoughts and afflictions
views.relation_to_self: The mind's own nature.
views.relation_to_world: Circumstances, including obstacles and death, are carried onto the path as one taste.
views.caveat: As for ult:kagyu.

names.name: Brahman (in its primary sense only Viṣṇu)

descriptions: the one independent reality; everything else is dependent on him (Tattvasaṅkhyāna 1)
free of all defects and full of all good qualities, each unlimited (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya, maṅgala)
known through the true scriptures alone, not by bare reasoning or the senses (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1)
source of the creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, knowledge, ignorance, bondage and release of the world (BSB 1.1.2)
of the nature of full bliss, knowledge and power; the fourfold Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, Turīya in all beings (Māṇḍūkya-bhāṣya)
his qualities, acts, forms and avatāras are identical with him; there is no internal difference in him (MBTN 1.69; VTN 3)
the primary meaning of every word and letter and the great purport of all scripture (BSB 1.1.1; VTN 1)
beyond the perishable (all souls) and the imperishable (Lakṣmī) (VTN 2)
negations: not without qualities — 'nirguṇa' means free of prakṛti's qualities (Karmanirṇaya)
not identical with the soul or the world; not their material cause
not subject to any defect, even in his descents (VTN 3)
not an attributeless consciousness — such a Brahman would be the Mādhyamika's void (Anuvyākhyāna 2.2.241–242)
views.relation_to_self: Eternally different from every soul; the soul is his reflection (pratibimba), wholly dependent on him, moved by him within, and in liberation enjoys its own bliss in his presence, desiring only in accord with his will and still graded and distinct.
views.relation_to_world: The world is real, eternally different from him and wholly dependent; he is its efficient cause and controller, prakṛti its material cause; he brings about its creation, maintenance, dissolution, bondage and release.
views.caveat: Dvaita affirms one supreme, independent reality and can read Ṛgveda 1.164.46 as 'the wise call the one (Viṣṇu) by many names', since for Madhva all names primarily denote Viṣṇu. It rejects any reading of 'one truth' as an identity in which souls, world and God are ultimately one; it rejects treating difference as provisional, empirical (vyāvahārika) or merely a standpoint; and it rejects placing other deities (Brahmā, Śiva and the rest, who are dependent souls) on a par with Viṣṇu as equal names of the supreme. Any reconciliation that dissolves the five differences is one the tradition explicitly refuses.

descriptions: By nature free of every fault, the single mass of all auspicious qualities, having the vyūhas as his limbs (Daśaślokī 4).
Worshipped with Rādhā, daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, on his left, served by thousands of sakhīs (Daśaślokī 5).
Both material and efficient cause through his powers; the controller of cit and acit, which are naturally different and non-different from him.
negations: Denies an attributeless (nirviśeṣa) Brahman.
Denies that difference is due to adjuncts.
views.relation_to_self: The soul is an atomic knower, part of the Lord, dependent on him, different and non-different by nature; liberated, it attains his nature without losing its distinctness.
views.relation_to_world: The world is real, a transformation of the Lord's power; acit is prākṛta, aprākṛta or time.
views.caveat: The school holds its dual-and-non-dual relation to be natural and eternal; it would reject a reading that collapses it into identity or into sheer difference.

names.name: the ground (gzhi): primordial purity and spontaneous presence
bodhicitta, the all-creating king (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)

descriptions: Essence empty (ngo bo stong pa), nature luminous (rang bzhin gsal ba), compassion all-pervading (thugs rje kun khyab) — the three aspects of the ground.
Primordially pure (ka dag) and spontaneously present (lhun grub).
'I am primordially self-arising wisdom, the essence of all phenomena' (Kunjed Gyalpo ch.4); the variety is non-dual, free of elaboration in its parts (Kunjed Gyalpo ch.31).
negations: not made, not to be sought, not attained by meditation (Kunjed Gyalpo ch.45)
beyond view, meditation, samaya, grounds and paths to traverse (Kunjed Gyalpo ch.44)
neither existent nor non-existent, free of the extremes (Longchenpa)
views.relation_to_self: Awareness is one's own nature; recognizing it is buddhahood, not recognizing it is the beginning of saṃsāra (one ground, two paths).
views.relation_to_world: Appearances arise as the ground's own display (rtsal, rol pa); deluded beings take them as external objects; in realization they self-liberate.
views.caveat: The 'all-creating king' of the Kunjed Gyalpo is awareness itself speaking, not a creator distinct from beings; Dzogchen also distinguishes the ground from the all-base (kun gzhi) and awareness from mind (sems), and would reject any identification of rig pa with a merely thoughtless state or with a Brahman-like self.

descriptions: Holds the parent school's view (ult:sakya).
views.caveat: Shares the Sakya view (see ult:sakya); no separate doctrine of the ultimate is claimed.

names.name: the unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned (ajāta, abhūta, akata, asaṅkhata)
the element of nibbāna with and without residue (saupādisesā / anupādisesā nibbānadhātu)
the further shore, the island, the refuge, the peaceful, the sublime (SN 43 synonyms)

descriptions: the destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion (SN 38.1)
the cessation of becoming (bhavanirodha) (SN 12.68)
the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation (MN 26; AN 3.32)
the highest happiness (Dhp 203–204); the deathless state (Dhp 21)
the unshakeable liberation of mind — 'unshakeable is my release; this is the last birth' (SN 56.11)
negations: there is that sphere where there is no earth, water, fire or air, no sphere of infinite space … no neither-perception-nor-non-perception, neither this world nor another, neither sun nor moon; no coming, going, staying, passing away or arising; without support, without occurrence, without object — this is the end of suffering (Ud 8.1)
there is an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned; were there not, no escape from the born, become, made, conditioned would be known (Ud 8.3)
consciousness that does not manifest (viññāṇaṃ anidassanaṃ), infinite, radiant all round, where earth, water, fire and air find no footing (DN 11; MN 49)
the Tathāgata released from reckoning by form … is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom like the ocean; 'is reborn', 'is not reborn', 'both', 'neither' do not apply (MN 72)
views.relation_to_self: Not a self and not the self's true nature: all conditioned things are impermanent and suffering, and 'all phenomena (sabbe dhammā) are not-self' (Dhp 277–279; AN 3.136). The ordinary person 'conceives nibbāna as mine, delights in nibbāna', the Tathāgata does not (MN 1).
views.relation_to_world: Not a cause, ground or source of the world: the world (loka), its origin, its cessation and the way to its cessation are declared 'in this fathom-long body with its perception and mind' (SN 2.26; AN 4.45). Nibbāna is the cessation of the world of the six senses, not what the world is made of.
views.caveat: The suttas speak of one unconditioned element (asaṅkhatā dhātu), but deny that it is a self, a creator, a Brahman or a metaphysical ground from which beings or the world proceed: the Brahmajāla (DN 1) lists the views that identify a permanent self or world as views born of contact and craving, and MN 1 criticises 'conceiving' even nibbāna. Any reading of nibbāna as 'the one reality called by many names' is an interpretation the tradition itself would reject if it implies a substantial essence; it accepts only that the same unconditioned is named by many epithets (SN 43).

descriptions: the eternal one whose form is Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, cause of all avatāras (Kīrtana-ghoṣā)
the root whose watering nourishes all the gods
views.relation_to_self: The soul is Kṛṣṇa's servant; the devotee seeks devotion, not liberation.
views.relation_to_world: Other gods and rites belong to the world; Kṛṣṇa alone is refuge.
views.caveat: The tradition itself refuses worship of other deities; it would reject a reconciliation that makes all deities equal objects of refuge, even while holding that worship of Kṛṣṇa satisfies all.

names.name: Īśvara, the Lord dwelling in the heart of all beings (18.61)
Vāsudeva, Keśava, Hari, Kṛṣṇa the lord of yoga (18.74–78)
Brahman — beginningless, supreme, imperishable (anādimat paraṃ brahma; akṣara)
Puruṣottama, the highest person beyond the perishable and the imperishable
Paramātman, the supreme self in the body
Īśvara / Maheśvara, the Lord dwelling in the heart of all beings
the twenty-sixth, the awakened (buddha), beyond the twenty-five

descriptions: the one from whom beings proceed and by whom all this is pervaded, to be worshipped with one's own work (18.46)
one imperishable being (bhāva) seen in all beings by sāttvic knowledge, undivided among the divided (18.20; the verse does not name it)
the Lord in the heart who makes all beings revolve by his māyā as if mounted on a machine (18.61)
known in truth by devotion — how great and who he is — and entered (18.55)
beginningless supreme Brahman, said to be neither being nor non-being (BhG 13.12)
with hands and feet everywhere, eyes, heads and faces everywhere, it stands enveloping all (13.13)
the light of lights beyond darkness, knowledge, the known and the goal of knowledge, seated in the heart of all (13.17)
that by which all this is pervaded is indestructible (2.17)
the highest Person who, entering the three worlds, sustains them (15.17–18)
the origin and dissolution of the whole world; all this is strung on him like pearls on a thread (7.6–7)
the knower of the field in all fields (13.2)
the twenty-sixth, ever awake, which the twenty-fifth comes to know (MBh 12.294–296)
views.relation_to_self: BhG 16–18: the Lord dwells in the bodies of all (16.18, 17.6) and in the heart of all beings (18.61); the one who has become brahman attains supreme devotion to him, knows him in truth and enters him (18.54–55).
views.relation_to_world: BhG 16–18: all this is pervaded by him and beings proceed from him (18.46); he moves all beings by his māyā (18.61); the demonic deny that the world has a Lord (16.8).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch16-18): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

negations: neither being nor non-being — na sat tan nāsad ucyate (BhG 13.12)
unmanifest, unthinkable, unchangeable (2.25)
weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it (2.23–24)
not seen with the ordinary eye, nor by Vedas, sacrifice, study or austerity, but by a divine eye or undivided devotion (11.8, 11.48, 11.53–54)
all beings abide in me but I do not abide in them — and yet beings do not abide in me (9.4–5)
the sun, moon and fire do not illumine that supreme abode (15.6)
views.caveat: The epic milieu is plural: it records Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Vedic, Pāñcarātra and Pāśupata views (MBh 12.337.59), differing counts of principles, and the question whether puruṣas are many or one (12.338). BhG 12.1–5 holds that worshippers of the unmanifest imperishable and of the Lord in form both reach him, the former with greater difficulty. Each Vedānta school reads the Gītā's ultimate in its own way and rejects the others' readings; the one-truth reading belongs to the interpretation layer, not to the epic's own text.

descriptions: 'The three realms are only mind; the myriad dharmas are only consciousness' as Fayan's guiding principle (Rentian yanmu).
negations: 'Not knowing is most intimate' (Luohan Guichen to Fayan).
views.relation_to_world: Every dharma bears the six characteristics of the Huayan teaching, total and particular at once.
views.caveat: Fayan uses Huayan categories but as Chan pointers.

names.name: phyag rgya chen po — Mahāmudrā: sūtra Mahāmudrā as emptiness, mantra Mahāmudrā as the clear light of great bliss
sems kyi gnas lugs — the abiding nature of mind

descriptions: The conventional nature of mind is clarity and knowing; its ultimate nature is its emptiness of inherent existence (Highway of the Conquerors, as the Gelug Mahāmudrā teaches).
Many names — co-emergent union, amulet box, fivefold, one taste, four letters, pacification, Chöd, Dzogchen, Madhyamaka view — converge in one intent (Highway of the Conquerors).
views.caveat: The 'one intent' is the emptiness of mind as the Gelug understands it (a non-affirming negation); the convergence statement is not a claim that the schools' views are identical in every detail.

descriptions: Lord of Satlok who appeared as Kabīr
negations: above the gods of the three worlds
views.relation_to_self: Freed by his Name.
views.relation_to_world: The three worlds are lower creation.
views.caveat: Low-confidence characterization.

names.name: Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya (Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa combined)

descriptions: The non-dual reality is called Brahman, Paramātman and Bhagavān (BhP 1.2.11); Bhagavān is its full manifestation.
Kṛṣṇa is the supreme Lord, whose form is being, consciousness and bliss, beginningless, the origin and cause of all causes (Brahma Saṃhitā 5.1).
The possessor of inconceivable powers (acintya-śakti), related to them in inconceivable difference-and-non-difference.
Rasa itself; most fully manifest in Vraja with Rādhā, his hlādinī-śakti.
negations: The impersonal Brahman is the effulgence of his body (Brahma Saṃhitā 5.40), an incomplete manifestation, not the highest.
Denies that his form is a product of māyā or that the world is vivarta.
views.relation_to_self: The soul is the Lord's marginal power (taṭasthā-śakti), an eternal servant, one with and different from him inconceivably (CC 2.20.108).
views.relation_to_world: The world is a real but temporary transformation of his external power (māyā-śakti); he himself remains unchanged, like the wish-fulfilling gem.
views.caveat: Gauḍīyas accept the three names of BhP 1.2.11 but grade them (Bhagavān fullest); they reject any reading that makes the personal form a provisional appearance of an impersonal Absolute.

names.name: stong pa nyid — emptiness of inherent existence (rang bzhin gyis stong pa)
don dam bden pa — ultimate truth
rten 'brel — dependent arising, the king of reasons
ngo bo nyid sku — the nature body (svābhāvikakāya)
'od gsal — the clear light (in Highest Yoga Tantra)

descriptions: The mere absence of inherent existence — of existence from the object's own side — in every phenomenon (Lamrim Chenmo, insight section).
Emptiness and dependent arising are one intention: because things arise dependently they are empty, and because empty they can arise (Three Principal Aspects 10–13; Praise of Dependent Origination).
The ultimate truth is an object of knowledge, found by a reasoning consciousness analysing the final mode of being.
negations: the object of negation is inherent existence, not conventional existence — negating too much falls into nihilism, too little into eternalism
emptiness is not an other-empty permanent absolute (against Dolpopa)
no ālaya-vijñāna and no reflexive awareness even conventionally (eight difficult points)
views.relation_to_self: The self exists merely as designated in dependence on the aggregates; the innate apprehension of an inherently existent self is the root of saṃsāra, cut only by the wisdom realizing its emptiness.
views.relation_to_world: The world exists conventionally, validly established by conventional valid cognition; cause and effect are 'unfailing' and fully compatible with emptiness.
views.caveat: Gelug holds that each phenomenon has its own emptiness (though all emptinesses are of one taste) and that emptiness is itself empty; it rejects any positive, self-existent absolute (shentong, Advaita's Brahman). It would accept 'one truth, many names' only for the single mode of being of all phenomena — their emptiness — not for a substance or a divine person.

names.name: the original mind shown as a circle (yuanxiang)

descriptions: 'In the ground of true reality not a single dust is accepted; in the gate of the myriad practices not a single dharma is discarded' (Guishan yulu).
negations: The circle-figures are to be burned once understood (Yangshan).
views.relation_to_world: Principle is realised suddenly; habit energies are removed gradually.
views.caveat: The circle is a pointer, not the thing (Yangshan burned the book of 97 circles).

names.name: Kuñjabihārī and Śyāmā, the natural pair (sahaja jorī)

descriptions: the pair eternally together in the grove, never joined and never parted
negations: not born, not separated, not newly united
views.relation_to_self: The devotee is a sakhī who serves and witnesses.
views.relation_to_world: The world's pursuits are empty; death is ever near; live as Hari keeps you.
views.caveat: The pair is held to be one reality in two forms; the tradition would reject an impersonal reading.

names.name: Śiva / Ādinātha, the guru whose nature is nāda, bindu and kalā
nirañjana, the stainless; paraṃ padam, the supreme state
parameśvara, the formless end of the tattvas
the one eternal knowledge without beginning or end (Śiva Saṃhitā 1.1)
Brahman as being, consciousness and bliss; the world full of Viṣṇu (Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā 7.4, 7.18)

descriptions: Whatever is heard as nāda is śakti; the formless end of the tattvas is the supreme Lord; the soundless is the supreme Brahman (HYP 4.101–102).
Stainless, unmoving, eternal, actionless, qualityless, great, consciousness of space, bliss (GŚ 99).
The supreme abode of Viṣṇu, where the mind dissolves within the resonance of the unstruck sound (HYP 4.100).
negations: niḥśabdam — soundless (HYP 4.101)
nirātaṅka, nirālamba, niṣprapañca, nirāśraya, nirāmaya, nirākāra (GŚ 92)
not smell, taste, form, touch or sound; neither self nor other (HYP 4.109)
views.relation_to_self: In samādhi the individual self and the supreme self become one, as salt dissolves in water (HYP 4.5–7); 'I am Brahman and no other' (GS 7.4).
views.relation_to_world: Duality is only what the mind sees; through unmanī it is not perceived (HYP 4.61); the world is the play of māyā (SS 1.64–67) — for the Vedāntic haṭha texts. The body is a microcosm of the world (SS 2.1–5).
views.caveat: The haṭha texts are practice manuals whose metaphysics is borrowed: Advaita in HYP 4 and Śiva Saṃhitā 1, a Vaiṣṇava theism joined to Advaita in the Gheraṇḍa, Śaiva in the Khecarīvidyā, Buddhist tantric in the Amṛtasiddhi. The HYP itself says of laya 'let this be called liberation or not' (4.30, 4.78), subordinating doctrine to attained state. The Amṛtasiddhi's Buddhist setting would not accept a Brahman–ātman reading of the one truth; the Amanaska subordinates all methods to the mindless state rather than to a named ultimate.

descriptions: 'Of the empty and calm mind, the numinous knowing is never obscured… the one word knowing is the gate of all wonders' (Zongmi reporting Heze teaching, Chan Preface).
negations: 'The true suchness is without thought' (Xianzong ji).
views.relation_to_self: It is one's true nature, known whether deluded or awakened.
views.caveat: Knowing is not discursive cognition; Zongmi insists it is not the same as seeing and hearing.

descriptions: The Absolute of Advaita, approached by yoga science (recalled; low confidence).
views.relation_to_self: The Self is Brahman.
views.relation_to_world: The world is appearance to be understood through practice.
views.caveat: Low-confidence summary; Swami Rama's books combine Advaita, Śrīvidyā and yoga.

descriptions: 'The Way needs no cultivation — only do not defile it… the ordinary mind is the Way' (Mazu's sermon, Jingde chuandeng lu juan 28).
'This very mind is buddha' (Mazu to Damei).
negations: 'Neither mind nor buddha' (Mazu).
views.relation_to_self: The very one walking, standing, sitting and lying.
views.relation_to_world: 'All dharmas are mind-dharmas; all names are mind-names' (Mazu).
views.caveat: Zongmi criticised Hongzhou for equating all activity with buddha-nature; Hongzhou would reject his charge (see dsp:hongzhou-all-activity-buddha-nature).

descriptions: The Absolute is prior to consciousness; the sense 'I am' is the first appearance, the door to it.
Nisargadatta: 'I am' is not the ultimate; the Absolute is beyond being and non-being.
views.relation_to_self: What one is, is the Absolute; the 'I am' is an appearance in it, dependent on the body.
views.relation_to_world: The world is an appearance in consciousness, which itself appears in the Absolute.
views.caveat: The lineage keeps devotional practice (bhajans, name-mantra) alongside a teaching that negates even consciousness; the one-truth reading must not drop the claim that the Absolute is beyond consciousness.

descriptions: The Absolute is Sachchidananda, which has involved itself in matter; the Supermind (Truth-Consciousness) is its creative power.
Both the materialist's denial of spirit and the ascetic's denial of matter are rejected.
views.relation_to_self: The psychic being is the evolving divine spark in the individual; the Self is one with the Divine.
views.relation_to_world: The world is real, a manifestation of the Divine, to be transformed rather than escaped.
views.caveat: Explicitly rejects Śaṅkara's reading of the world as illusion; reconciliation with Advaita must record that rejection.

names.name: Paramātman (the supreme self, the soul fully manifest)
the soul's own nature (svabhāva) with its infinite fourfold

descriptions: the soul's own nature fully unveiled: infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy
who knows one knows all; who knows all knows one (Ācārāṅga 1.3.4)
formless being that perceives and knows, beyond comparison (Ācārāṅga 1.5.6)
abiding at the summit of the universe in unobstructed happiness (Aupapātika; Uttarādhyayana 36)
the pure, eternal law is non-harm, proclaimed by all Arhats (Ācārāṅga 1.4.1)
Each soul's own pure nature: infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy, manifest when all karma is shed (TS 10.2–4).
The liberated soul abides at the summit of the universe, bodiless, knowing all substances and all modes (TS 1.29, 10.5).
Called by others Sadāśiva, the supreme Brahman, the perfected self, suchness — one goal under many names (Haribhadra, YDS 129–130).
Non-violence is called the supreme Brahman known in the world (Svayambhūstotra, recalled).
negations: not long or short, of no colour, smell, taste or touch; not female, male or neuter; beyond sound, reasoning and mind (Ācārāṅga 1.5.6)
not a creator or ruler of the world
not a single substance of which souls are parts
No creator or controller of the world (Ādipurāṇa 4; Anyayogavyavacchedikā 6).
Not one all-pervading self: souls are innumerable, distinct and body-sized (TS 5.16).
Not merely permanent nor merely momentary (TS 5.30).
views.relation_to_self: Every soul is by nature what the Siddha is; bondage is karmic matter covering that nature, and liberation is its uncovering by one's own effort through the three jewels.
views.relation_to_world: The world is real, uncreated and eternal, made of souls and non-souls; the liberated know it entirely but neither make nor govern it.
views.caveat: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator: liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct, and the universe of six substances is uncreated. It can accept 'one truth, many names' only in its own way — as many-sidedness (anekānta) about a plural reality — not as the identity of all souls in one substance.
views.notes: U35 contribution (lin:jainism is owned by U34, which may add its own view under the same id; the merge unions them).

names.name: the name Namu Amida Butsu (as itself birth)

descriptions: The birth of all beings was settled as 'Namu Amida Butsu' at Amida's perfect awakening ten kalpas ago (Kumano oracle, as reported in the Ippen Hijiri-e).
In the nenbutsu the self, the Buddha and the name are not separate; the name recites the name (reported sayings).
views.relation_to_self: The self is to be cast off; not even faith is to be relied on as one's own.
views.relation_to_world: Everything — mountains, rivers, grasses, the sound of wind and waves — is the nenbutsu (reported sayings, Goroku).
views.caveat: Ippen's sayings survive mainly in later compilations; the view is reconstructed from them (low confidence on wording).

descriptions: the gnosis that is the nature of the deity, realized by the union of the two stages
views.relation_to_self: The practitioner generates himself as Mañjuvajra; the deity is the purified nature.
views.relation_to_world: Appearances are the display of gnosis (maṇḍala).
views.caveat: Reconstructed from general knowledge of the school; no Jñānapāda text read locally.

names.name: Amida Nyorai; the Tathāgata of Unhindered Light filling the ten directions (Jin jippō mugekō nyorai)

descriptions: The supreme Buddha is formless; being formless it is called jinen; Amida is the means by which we are made to know jinen (the jinen hōni letter).
The true Buddha is the Tathāgata of inconceivable light; the true land is the land of immeasurable light (Kyōgyōshinshō, chapter on the true Buddha and land).
Shinjin is buddha-nature; buddha-nature is the Tathāgata (Jōdo wasan; Kyōgyōshinshō, Shin chapter).
negations: Birth is not attained by the practitioner's calculation (hakarai); 'no working is true working'.
views.relation_to_self: The self is a foolish being full of blind passions for whom no practice is possible; shinjin, given by Amida, is itself the Buddha's mind in the person, who becomes 'equal to the Tathāgatas' while remaining a foolish being.
views.relation_to_world: The world is a burning house where 'all is empty and false; only the nenbutsu is true' (Tannishō postscript); one returns to it from the Pure Land to save others (gensō).
views.caveat: Shinshū distinguishes sharply between the Buddha's mind and the foolish being's mind, and between the true and transformed lands; it would reject any reading that makes the practitioner already a buddha by his own realization or that treats Amida as one deity among many worthy of worship.

names.name: Gokuraku jōdo (the Land of Utmost Bliss)
the name Namu Amida Butsu, in which all virtues are gathered

descriptions: The name contains all the virtues of the Buddha's inner realization and outer activity; hence it is superior and was selected in the primal vow (Senchakushū 3).
Amida is a reward-body buddha in a reward land to which ordinary beings are born by the power of the vow (following Shandao).
views.relation_to_self: The practitioner is an ignorant ordinary being who should, like one who knows not a single letter, simply say the nenbutsu (One-Sheet Document).
views.relation_to_world: This world in the last age is to be left; the Pure Land in the west is where awakening is completed; one lives so as best to say the nenbutsu.
views.caveat: Jōdo-shū keeps 'pointing to a direction and establishing form' (shihō rissō) and rejects readings of the Pure Land as mind only; it would not accept reducing Amida to an impersonal absolute.

names.name: buddha-nature, the essence of the sugatas (bde gshegs snying po)
the emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects (rnam kun mchog ldan gyi stong nyid)
Kālacakra, the primordial buddha (dus kyi 'khor lo, dang po'i sangs rgyas)

descriptions: permanent, stable, peaceful and eternal (rtag brtan ther zug g.yung drung)
self-arisen primordial wisdom, luminous, non-dual
endowed from the beginning with the inseparable buddha-qualities, which are uncovered, not produced
pervading all beings as space pervades
not a dependent arising; beyond the three times
possessing the perfections of purity, bliss, self and permanence (RGV 1.35 read as definitive)
negations: empty of the adventitious stains — every conventional phenomenon — which are other than it
not empty of its own nature
not the mere non-affirming negation, the 'emptiness of annihilation' (chad stong) that is nothing whatsoever
views.relation_to_self: The dharmakāya is the true self in the sense of the perfection of self; the imputed self of persons and phenomena does not exist. Buddha-nature is complete in every being.
views.relation_to_world: The world of conventional phenomena is empty of its own nature, false and adventitious; it is 'other' than the ultimate, which it obscures but never taints.
views.caveat: The Jonang affirm one ultimate, but insist that it is other than conventional phenomena and deny that the rangtong emptiness (mere absence of inherent existence) is the final ultimate. The rangtong schools — Gelug (Tsongkhapa, Khedrup), the Sakya scholar Gorampa and many others — reject a non-empty, permanent ultimate as the extreme of eternalism, close to the tīrthikas' self; the Jonang reject the equation of their dharmakāya with a tīrthika ātman. Not yet reconciled: see dsp:rangtong-shentong.

names.name: Brahman, unthinkable and unmanifest, without and with qualities (Sūrya Siddhānta 1.1)
Vāsudeva, the supreme Brahman; Aniruddha as the Sun-Hiraṇyagarbha (SS 12.12–21)
Ka — one and many, the true deity, the supreme Brahman (Āryabhaṭīya 1.1)
Viṣṇu, one and unmanifest, with the powers Śrī, Bhū and Nīlā; Janārdana in the form of the planets (BPHS 1.9–20; 2.3)
The Sun as self of all embodied beings, self of Kālapuruṣa, maker of time and door of liberation (Yogayātrā 1.1; BJ 1.1; 2.1)
Kāla, time — the destroyer of worlds (SS 1.10)

descriptions: acintya-avyakta-rūpa, nirguṇa yet guṇātman, support of the world (SS 1.1)
one quarter manifest, three quarters immortal (SS 12.20; BPHS 1.10–11)
present in all beings as the supreme-Self portion beside the jīva-portion (BPHS 1.21–24)
gives beings the fruits of karma in the form of the planets (BPHS 2.3)
negations: unthinkable, unmanifest, without qualities (SS 1.1)
time without beginning or end (Āryabhaṭīya 3.11)
views.relation_to_self: The Sun is the self of Kālapuruṣa and of all embodied beings (BJ 2.1; Yogayātrā 1.1); each being has a portion of the individual soul and a portion of the supreme Self (BPHS 1.21–24); the ātmakāraka signifies the self in the chart.
views.relation_to_world: The Lord divides himself into the twelve signs and twenty-seven asterisms (SS 12.25); time is his form; the planets are his forms and avatāras dispensing karma (BPHS 2.3–7); the earth-globe stands in space by Brahman's supporting power (SS 12.32).
views.caveat: Jyotiṣa is a limb (aṅga) of the Veda — its eye — and a science of time and of the ripening of karma, not itself a soteriology. It names the ultimate only in invocations and in cosmogonies borrowed from Pāñcarātra, Purāṇic and Vedāntic frames, and different texts invoke different ultimates (Brahman, Vāsudeva, Viṣṇu, the Sun, Ka); it would not claim that reading or remedying the chart liberates, though horā names the configurations that indicate liberation (BJ 25.15; Jaimini 1.2.69). A one-truth reading should not be read back into it as its own doctrine.

names.name: Rām / the one known by pārakh

descriptions: what remains when every doctrine has been tested as the mind's creation
negations: no god of the books
no name that can be written
views.relation_to_self: The discerning self is not deceived by the gods and doctrines the mind makes.
views.relation_to_world: The world of doctrines is the mind's; delusion (bhram) is to be dissolved.
views.caveat: The Pārakh reading (Pūran Sāhib) borders on declining to posit any ultimate beyond discernment itself; recorded as a low-confidence characterization.

descriptions: the True Being of Satlok, beyond the three worlds
incarnate as Kabīr in every age
negations: not Kāl Nirañjan, the creator of the three worlds
not Brahmā, Viṣṇu or Maheś
views.relation_to_self: The soul (haṃs) is of the Sat Puruṣ's substance, fallen under Kāl, and returns to Satlok by the true Name.
views.relation_to_world: The three worlds are Kāl's creation and prison; Satlok alone is true.
views.caveat: The Kabīr Panth's cosmogony and its worship of Kabīr as God sit uneasily with the Bījak's apophatic critique; the Kabīr Chaurā and Pārakh readings stress discernment over mythology.

names.name: don dam bden pa (ultimate truth), one only

descriptions: The ultimate is one; others hold it to be two; dharmatā, established as nothing at all, cannot be two or three (Satyadvayāvatāra 4).
Without arising or ceasing; free of thing and non-thing; inexpressible, unconditioned; realizing it the yogin abandons the afflictive and cognitive obscurations (Satyadvayāvatāra 5–9).
Wisdom is knowing the emptiness of own-nature of aggregates, elements and sense-bases as unborn (Bodhipathapradīpa v48).
negations: no arising from self, other, both or without cause (Bodhipathapradīpa v50)
not found when analysed as one or many (Bodhipathapradīpa v51)
seeing it is 'not seeing'; no seer and nothing seen (Satyadvayāvatāra 7)
views.relation_to_self: Selflessness of persons and phenomena; the practitioner meditates on selflessness without conceptualization (Bodhipathapradīpa v54–55).
views.relation_to_world: Conventional truth is of two kinds, false and correct; correct conventional truth is what, unexamined, arises and ceases and can perform functions; it is to be respected — cause and effect, virtue and vice — and is the ladder to the ultimate (Satyadvayāvatāra 2–3, 18–22).
views.caveat: Atiśa's 'the ultimate is one' denies that the ultimate is divisible, not that it is a single substance: it is dharmatā 'not established as anything'. A reading of it as a positive one-reality would be rejected.

descriptions: Holds the parent school's view (ult:kadam).
views.caveat: Shares the Kadam view (see ult:kadam).

descriptions: Holds the parent school's view (ult:kadam).
views.caveat: Shares the Kadam view (see ult:kadam).

descriptions: Holds the parent school's view (ult:kadam).
views.caveat: Shares the Kadam view (see ult:kadam).

names.name: Mahāmudrā (phyag rgya chen po, 'the great seal')
the nature of mind; mind-as-such (sems nyid)
co-emergent wisdom (lhan cig skyes pa'i ye shes)
ordinary mind (tha mal gyi shes pa)

descriptions: One's own mind, luminous (clear) and empty, unborn, beyond colour, shape and location, like space (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā; Nāropa's Dṛṣṭisaṃkṣipta).

The union of clarity and emptiness, of appearance and emptiness, of bliss and emptiness — 'neither existent, for even the victors do not see it, nor non-existent, for it is the basis of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa' (3rd Karmapa's Aspiration Prayer).
Its emptiness is the dharmakāya, its unceasing radiance the nirmāṇakāya, their union great bliss the saṃbhogakāya (Karṇatantravajrapada).
The nature of thought is dharmakāya; appearances are the light of the dharmakāya.
negations: not an existent thing: 'even the victors do not see it'
not nothing: it is the basis of all saṃsāra and nirvāṇa
beyond speech, thought and expression; cannot be shown (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā v1)
not a self (ātman) or a primordial nature (pradhāna) as the tīrthikas hold (Dṛṣṭisaṃkṣipta)
views.relation_to_self: The ultimate is one's own mind's nature, not something to be sought elsewhere; the 'self' grasped by beings is the delusion that obscures it; buddha-nature is present in all beings as the cause of awakening.
views.relation_to_world: Appearances are mind's own display, appearing yet empty like a moon in water; saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are that same mind obscured or freed of adventitious stains.
views.caveat: The Kagyu would reject reading 'mind's nature' as a single substance, a creator, or an eternal self in the Vedāntic sense: it is empty of any intrinsic existence and is realized, not posited. Vajradhara, from whom the lineage descends, is the dharmakāya in personal form for the lineage, not a creator. 'One taste' is the yogin's realization that appearances and mind are not two, not a monist ontology.

names.name: Kālacakra (time and wheel = means and wisdom)

descriptions: the image arisen from emptiness is the cause; the bliss born of the immutable is the result; each seals the other (Sekoddeśa 146)
the fourth consecration is the ultimate, the other three are conventional (Sekoddeśa 8)
negations: the stain of mind is neither adventitious nor long-lasting, neither born without mind nor abiding in it (Sekoddeśa 129)
views.relation_to_self: Kālacakra is the non-dual union within the practitioner's body of the unchanging bliss and the empty form of the deity.
views.relation_to_world: Outer (cosmos, time), inner (body) and alternative (deity) wheels correspond; the practitioner reverses the movement of time in the channels.
views.caveat: The Vimalaprabhā insists that the Ādibuddha is not a creator god and not a self; it is emptiness endowed with all aspects.

descriptions: Inscriptions praise Kālāmukha ācāryas as devotees of Śiva and masters of the Lakula-siddhānta; no Kālāmukha doctrinal treatise survives.
views.relation_to_self: Not recorded in the tradition's own words.
views.relation_to_world: Not recorded in the tradition's own words.
views.caveat: Known only from inscriptions and from opponents (Yāmuna, Rāmānuja).

descriptions: she who devours (kalana) Mahākāla, the devourer of all beings; the beginning of all (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32)
black because every colour disappears in black as all beings enter Kālī (Mahānirvāṇa 13.5-6)
pure consciousness, witness of all, watching Time play (Mahānirvāṇa 13.12)
the Śakti without whom Sadāśiva is a corpse (Toḍala 1.25)
negations: formless (arūpā): her form is imagined according to her qualities and acts (Mahānirvāṇa 5.140)
the formless meditation on her is beyond speech and mind (Mahānirvāṇa 5.137-138)
views.relation_to_self: The worshipper is to see all as Brahman ('sarvaṃ brahmamayam', Mahānirvāṇa 3.120, 8.175); in the devotional Kālī tradition the self is her child, and in the Kaula view the bound jīva is Śiva himself (Kulārṇava 9.42).
views.relation_to_world: The worlds arise from her and return into her as colours into black; she creates, sustains and devours, and is the Mother of Time (Mahānirvāṇa 5.140; 13.5-8).
views.caveat: The Kālī tantras make the Goddess the source of Śiva, Brahmā and Viṣṇu (Nirvāṇa Tantra) and treat Viṣṇu's avatāras as her forms (Toḍala 10); they accept a one-truth reading only with her as that truth. The devotional tradition resists dissolving her motherhood into an impersonal absolute.

descriptions: The soul in its niścaya nature is pure knowing, untouched by karma; there is no creator God.
views.relation_to_self: Each soul is eternally distinct, and in its true nature already pure (niścaya).
views.relation_to_world: Six real substances (dravya) with their own modifications; no substance acts on another.
views.caveat: As a Jain school it denies a single creator or a single world-soul; the one-truth reading applies only to the common nature of all souls, and the tradition would reject any identity of souls.

names.name: Soma (Śiva 'with Umā'; name of the doctrine Somasiddhānta)

descriptions: Worshipped as Mahābhairava (Prabodhacandrodaya act 3, an opponent's portrayal).
Kapālin: the skull-bearing form of Śiva whose penance for Brahmā's head the Kāpālika imitates (Kūrma P. 2.31).
views.relation_to_self: Yāmuna reports that for the Kāpālikas liberation comes from knowing and wearing the six insignia and from a meditation on the self, not from knowledge of Brahman (opponent's report).
views.relation_to_world: Not recorded in the tradition's own words.
views.caveat: Known almost entirely through opponents and satirists; no Kāpālika scripture has been identified with certainty. Somasiddhānta, the name of their doctrine, is attested; its content is not.

descriptions: The ground of purification is mind itself, clarity and emptiness inseparable; the purifier is the vajra yoga of Mahāmudrā; the purified are the adventitious stains; the fruit is the stainless dharmakāya (3rd Karmapa).
The eight consciousnesses, recognized, are the five wisdoms (Distinguishing Consciousness and Wisdom).
negations: neither existent nor non-existent; free of the extremes
views.relation_to_self: Buddha-nature is the beginningless element present in every being, obscured by adventitious stains.
views.relation_to_world: Appearances are mind; mind is empty; emptiness is not a blank but luminous.
views.caveat: The school holds two readings of how buddha-nature is empty — as empty of own-nature (the 8th Karmapa's Madhyamaka) or as empty only of what is other than it (the shentong reading of the 8th Situ and Jamgön Kongtrul) — not yet reconciled (dsp:rangtong-shentong).

descriptions: the one Master present in the living guru
hidden in the human form
negations: not the many gods of outward custom
views.relation_to_self: The Kartā is found in the human, above all the guru.
views.relation_to_world: Outward custom is kept for the world's sake; the truth is secret.
views.caveat: The tradition's double life means its outward Hindu observances should not be read as its view of the ultimate.

descriptions: light (prakāśa) inseparable from self-reflexive awareness (vimarśa)
perfect I-ness (pūrṇāhantā)
absolutely free (svatantra); cause of the world's establishment (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya 1)
endowed with the powers cit, ānanda, icchā, jñāna, kriyā
performs the five acts
contains the universe as a mirror contains its images (Paramārthasāra 12-13)
negations: not the ninefold, not the mass of sounds, not three-headed, not composed of nāda and bindu (Vijñāna Bhairava 11-12)
free from the reckoning of space and time, indescribable in the supreme sense (VBT 14)
views.relation_to_self: Identical: 'consciousness is the self' (Śiva Sūtra 1.1); the individual is Śiva contracted (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya 4, 9), to be recognized as the Lord (ĪPK 1.1.1-3).
views.relation_to_world: The world is Śiva's own free self-manifestation unfolded on his own screen (PH 2); real as his manifestation, not an illusion and not other than him.
views.caveat: The tradition insists that the ultimate is active (vimarśa, svātantrya, the five acts) and that the world is real as its manifestation; it rejects readings of its absolute as an inactive witness or of the world as unreal appearance (Advaita), and it rejects the grammarians' paśyantī as the highest (Śivadṛṣṭi 2).

descriptions: Śiva, the supreme Brahman, partless, all-knowing, the doer of all, pure, non-dual, self-luminous, without beginning or end, without qualities, being–consciousness–bliss (Kulārṇava 1.7-8)
the bliss (ānanda) born of the union of Śakti and Śiva is called liberation (Kulārṇava 5.79)
