bliss is the form of Brahman, and it abides in the body (Kulārṇava 5.80)
negations: beyond both duality and non-duality (Kulārṇava 1.110)
views.relation_to_self: The individual souls are parts of Śiva like sparks of a fire, covered by beginningless ignorance (Kulārṇava 1.8-9); bound by fetters the self is jīva, freed it is Sadāśiva (Kulārṇava 9.42-43).
views.relation_to_world: Kula is Śakti — the totality of powers and of the manifest — and Akula is Śiva; the Kaula joins both (Kulārṇava 17.27).
views.caveat: The Kaula texts refuse to be classed as dualist or non-dualist (Kulārṇava 1.110) and insist that the truth is realised through the guru's transmission and Kula practice, not by learning (1.96-100); a purely doctrinal one-truth reading leaves out the ritual and lineage conditions they make essential.

descriptions: Tripurā is the fusion of prakāśa and vimarśa (Dīpikā on YH 1.6).
The kāmakalā — two bindus, white and red, and their union — is the Goddess's own form; knowing it one becomes Mahātripurasundarī (Kāmakalāvilāsa 6-8).
views.relation_to_self: Knowledge of the cakra-saṅketa makes one liberated while living, abiding in the I-sense of Śiva (YH 1.86 with the Dīpikā).
views.relation_to_world: The cakra of thirty-six principles unfolds when Śakti beholds her own vibrancy (YH 1.9-10).
views.caveat: This line holds the Goddess is both Kaula and Samaya and that outer worship is part of the path even for the knower; it would not accept a Samaya reconciliation that declares Kaula worship outside the Veda.

names.name: the seven installed deities as forms of the supreme

descriptions: From the supreme Lord endowed with existence, consciousness and bliss, and with parts (sakala), arose Śakti; from her Nāda; from Nāda, Bindu (Śāradātilaka 1.7).
views.caveat: Kerala tantra is a ritual tradition serving several deities; it has no single systematic theology. The Prapañcasāra (attributed to Śaṅkara) frames mantra practice non-dualistically, while the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati follows Śaiva Siddhānta.

descriptions: one's own consciousness, whose free and independent variety is the supreme Goddess (TĀ 4.172)
the power that projects, knows, counts, moves and sounds (TĀ 4.173)
the final Kālī in whom full consciousness dissolves into the Akula abode (TĀ 4.170)
negations: the nameless (anākhya)
views.relation_to_self: The goddess is one's own consciousness (svasaṃvid).
views.relation_to_world: The Kālīs emit, hold and devour the world as phases of cognition across object, means and subject.
views.caveat: Known chiefly through Abhinavagupta, Jayaratha and Maheśvarānanda; the Krama stresses the sequence of the goddess's phases as the way into the sequenceless and would resist a reading that erases the sequence.

descriptions: Krishnamacharya, a Śrīvaiṣṇava, taught devotion to the Lord (Īśvara-praṇidhāna) as the summit of yoga (recalled; low confidence).
views.relation_to_self: The seer (puruṣa) distinct from the mind, devoted to the Lord.
views.relation_to_world: The world real, the field of practice.
views.caveat: Most of the lineage's students taught āsana without a fixed metaphysics; this view represents Krishnamacharya himself only.

descriptions: Sri Yukteswar: God is the one eternal substance, from whom the Word (Aum) and creation proceed.
Yogananda: Self-realization is knowing in body, mind and soul one's oneness with the omnipresence of God.
views.relation_to_self: The soul is an individualized reflection of Spirit; Self-realization reveals oneness with God.
views.relation_to_world: Creation is God's dream and light; the cycle of yugas shapes human understanding.
views.caveat: The lineage harmonizes Hindu and Christian scripture; a one-truth reading suits it but it would keep God's personal aspect and the guru's role.

descriptions: the supreme power of knowledge, will and action, straight as a line and again coiled like a sleeping serpent, the power of sound (Kubjikāmata 2.2, hymn)
the supreme primal yoni of the supreme, fourfold as beyond form, form, word and body (Kubjikāmata 11.6-7)
dark as collyrium, bent, both beautiful and deformed, of many forms (Kubjikāmata 2.4-5)
negations: beyond form (rūpātīta) at its highest level (Kubjikāmata 11.7)
views.relation_to_self: The Goddess is the coiled power within the practitioner's body, located in the six centres; the initiate receives her command (ājñā) through the guru lineage.
views.relation_to_world: The world is born within the sixfold order of the Goddess (Kubjikāmata 11.13-16); Bhairava and she are cause and effect of one another (2.17-18).
views.caveat: The Kubjikā ultimate is expressed through a secret mantra-maṇḍala system and lineage command; the tradition treats this knowledge as unshareable outside initiation, so any one-truth equation is at most an outer reading.

descriptions: Consciousness is the Self (Śiva Sūtra 1.1 as he taught it); Śiva with his energy of freedom (svātantrya) manifests the universe.
views.relation_to_self: The individual is Śiva who has forgotten himself; recognition restores it.
views.relation_to_world: The universe is real as the manifestation of Śiva's own energy.
views.caveat: Follows Kashmir Śaivism's rejection of the world's unreality (cf. U19's view).

descriptions: The Svacchanda Tantra says the skull-observers and the Pāśupatas stand 'in the Īśvara and in the Dhruva' and are not re-created (11.184); the Lākula goal is thus described by others as a fixed level beyond rebirth.
views.relation_to_self: Not recorded in the tradition's own words.
views.relation_to_world: Not recorded in the tradition's own words; scholarship reports an expanded hierarchy of worlds.
views.caveat: Reconstructed entirely from others' texts; any statement of the Lākula view of the ultimate is provisional.

descriptions: the unconditioned ultimate reality of the Abhidhamma, to be realized in this very life by insight developed through the thirty-seven requisites of awakening
views.relation_to_self: no self; the belief in self (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) is the first thing to be removed
views.relation_to_world: the cessation of the round of rebirth
views.caveat: Ledi's writings keep to the commentarial Abhidhamma: nibbāna is not a ground of being or a self.

names.name: true person of no rank (wuwei zhenren 無位真人)
person of the Way who depends on nothing (wuyi daoren 無依道人)

descriptions: 'On the lump of red flesh there is a true person of no rank, always going in and out of the gates of your face' (Linji lu).
'The mind-dharma has no form and pervades the ten directions; in the eye it is called seeing, in the ear hearing…' (Linji lu).
'Only the person of the Way who depends on nothing, listening to the Dharma, is the mother of all buddhas' (Linji lu).
negations: 'What kind of dried shit-stick is the true person of no rank?' (Linji lu) — no fixation even of this.
views.relation_to_self: It is 'just you, listening to the Dharma right in front of me'.
views.relation_to_world: Entering all realms — ordinary and holy, pure and defiled — without being defined by them; 'be master wherever you are'.
views.caveat: Linji denies that any name — buddha, patriarch, bodhi, nirvāṇa — is the reality; they are 'hitching posts for donkeys'. The tradition would reject reifying the true person as a soul.

descriptions: Everything about the Buddhas is beyond the world — conduct, merit, postures, body, robes, food (Mvu i.167–168).
They conform to the world only for beings' sake (Mvu i.168–169).
negations: Nothing about the perfect Buddhas is like the world (Mvu i.159).
views.relation_to_self: The aggregates are not self (Mvu iii.335).
views.relation_to_world: The Buddha's worldly life is a display conforming to worldly convention.
views.caveat: The supramundane is predicated of the Buddhas and their qualities, not of a single cosmic ground; the tradition would not equate it with Brahman or a self.

descriptions: not dependent on another, peaceful, not elaborated by elaborations, free of conceptual construction, without multiplicity — the mark of reality (MMK 18.9)
dependent origination, qualified by the eight negations, the pacification of elaborations, auspicious (MMK dedicatory verses)
the pacification of all apprehending, the pacification of elaboration, auspicious (MMK 25.24)
the emptiness which is dependent origination, which is a dependent designation and the middle way (MMK 24.18)
negations: no cessation, no arising, no annihilation, no permanence, no unity, no plurality, no coming, no going (dedication)
not arisen from self, other, both or no cause (MMK 1.1)
nirvāṇa is neither an existent nor a non-existent (MMK 25.4–10)
'empty' should not be said, nor 'not empty', nor both, nor neither — they are said only for designation (MMK 22.11)
emptiness is itself empty; it is not a view (MMK 13.8; 24.18)
views.relation_to_self: The self is not identical with the aggregates nor different from them (MMK 18.1; 27.4–8); it is a designation made in dependence on them, like a chariot on its parts (MA 6.150ff). Knowing reality is the ceasing of 'I' and 'mine' (MMK 18.2–4).
views.relation_to_world: Emptiness is not another thing behind the world: it is the world's being dependently arisen (MMK 24.18–19). The limit of nirvāṇa is the limit of saṃsāra (MMK 25.19–20). The world is accepted as conventional truth, and the ultimate is taught only by relying on it (MMK 24.10).
views.caveat: Madhyamaka rejects any reading of emptiness as a positive ultimate entity, ground, substance or absolute — it is the mere absence of own-nature in each thing and is itself empty; to take it as a view or a thing is called incurable (MMK 13.8). Calling emptiness 'the one truth named variously' would be admitted only as a conventional designation, not as naming a real referent. The school also rejects identification with the Upaniṣadic brahman or ātman (Madhyamakahṛdaya ch.8; Tattvasaṅgraha).

descriptions: the one Supreme, distinct from souls, deities and world, who alone liberates and incarnates as the five Kṛṣṇas
negations: not any of the devatās
not the world
views.relation_to_self: Souls are eternally distinct from Parameśvara and are liberated by his grace.
views.relation_to_world: The world (prapañca) is an eternal reality of māyā, distinct from him.
views.caveat: The Mahānubhāvas insist on the distinctness of Parameśvara from the Vedic and Purāṇic gods and from souls; they reject the identification of all gods as forms of one truth.

descriptions: The Buddhas are supramundane, without outflows, limitless in body, power and life, always in concentration (Vasumitra).
The mind is by nature luminous, defiled by adventitious defilements (Vasumitra).
negations: Past and future are not real entities (Vasumitra).
views.relation_to_self: No self is affirmed; the luminous nature of mind is not called a self.
views.relation_to_world: The Buddha only appears to live in the world; nine unconditioned dharmas are counted (low confidence).
views.caveat: Known almost only through opponents' and later doxographies; the Mahāsāṃghika does not identify the luminous mind or the Buddha with a cosmic single reality.

descriptions: experienced at the path and fruition moments as the cessation of all formations noted up to that point; afterwards it can be re-entered as fruition attainment
views.relation_to_self: noting reveals only arising and passing processes, no self who notes
views.relation_to_world: the cessation of the noted object and the noting mind
views.caveat: The tradition describes nibbāna by the knowledges leading to it, not as a metaphysical ground.

names.name: sahaja (lhan cig skyes pa, the innate / co-emergent)

descriptions: mind itself alone is the seed of everything, from which saṃsāra and nirvāṇa radiate; it grants what is wished like a wish-fulfilling jewel (People Dohā v42–43)
the innate is the Buddha dwelling in the body (People Dohā v82)
like space: beyond colour and shape, unstained by good and evil (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā v11)
negations: not thing and not no-thing (People Dohā v21–22)
cannot be told in words (People Dohā v39)
views.relation_to_self: The innate is realized when self and other are not distinguished (People Dohā v73, v98); Saraha's 'self' (bdag nyid) language is not an ātman doctrine but the nature of mind.
views.relation_to_world: Whatever is seen in front, behind and in the ten directions is 'that itself' (People Dohā v29); saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not two (People Dohā v122).
views.caveat: The siddhas point to the nature of mind rather than to a being; their 'one' is the non-duality of appearance and emptiness, and they would reject both an eternal self and a mere nothingness.

descriptions: the one unconditioned dhamma among the four ultimate realities (citta, cetasika, rūpa, nibbāna)
single in its own nature (sabhāva) but described as with residue (sa-upādisesa) and without residue (anupādisesa), and as empty, signless and desireless
an object (ārammaṇa) of the path and fruition consciousness, not a mere absence
negations: not arisen, not ageing, not dying (asaṅkhata)
not a self: 'there is extinction, but no one extinguished' (Vism XVI, PTS p. 513)
views.relation_to_self: no self is found in or behind it; all dhammas including nibbāna are not-self
views.relation_to_world: the cessation of the conditioned; entirely transcending the world of the five aggregates
views.caveat: The commentarial tradition would reject any reading of nibbāna as a cosmic ground, a creator or a self; the 'one truth' reading applies only in the sense that nibbāna is the single unconditioned element.

descriptions: the suchness of the Tathāgata and the suchness of all dharmas are one suchness, undivided (Aṣṭasāhasrikā 16)
the Tathāgata is non-arising, the reality-limit, emptiness, suchness — which neither come nor go (Aṣṭa 31)
all dharmas have the mark of emptiness: unborn, unceasing, not defiled, not pure, not deficient, not complete (Heart, s6)
the Tathāgata is to be seen from the dharma; the guides have the dharma for body; dharmatā cannot be cognized (Vajracchedikā 26)
the one buddha-vehicle (Lotus 2); the Tathāgata's lifespan is immeasurable (Lotus 16)
entry into non-duality is Vimalakīrti's silence, where there is no movement of letters, sounds or ideas (Vimalakīrti 8.33)
negations: not the least dharma is found in anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi — therefore it is called so (Vajracchedikā 22)
even nirvāṇa is like an illusion, like a dream; if there were anything higher than nirvāṇa that too would be like an illusion (Aṣṭa 2)
in emptiness there is no form ... no suffering, origin, cessation, path; no knowing and no attaining (Heart s6-7)
not existent, not non-existent; the middle between 'is' and 'is not' (Kāśyapaparivarta §60)
views.relation_to_self: Persons and dharmas are both without self (pudgala- and dharma-nairātmya); the bodhisattva who has the notion of a self, a being, a soul or a person is not a bodhisattva (Vajracchedikā 3, 14). Some sūtras nonetheless name the buddha-nature 'self' (see ult:tathagatagarbha).
views.relation_to_world: The world is empty, dependently arisen, like an illusion, dream or reflection; it is not annihilated either. Form is emptiness and emptiness is form (Heart s4); saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not two (Vimalakīrti 8); the purity of a buddha-field follows the purity of the mind (Vimalakīrti 1.14).
views.caveat: The Prajñāpāramitā denies that emptiness, suchness or nirvāṇa is an entity or a substance: they are 'names only', to be neither grasped nor rejected, and 'the view of emptiness' is itself declared incurable (Kāśyapaparivarta §64-65). The sūtras also speak of the Buddha's eternal dharmakāya and of compassionate buddhas and bodhisattvas, which is why 'both' is recorded; they reject any creator god and any reading of suchness as a Brahman-like self (Laṅkāvatāra p. 33, on the tīrthikas' ātman).

descriptions: God is formless, beyond writing and description, the void (śūnya) that is full.
views.relation_to_self: All beings belong to Alekha; devotion and surrender to him.
views.relation_to_world: The world is his creation; images are false.
views.caveat: The tradition rejects image worship and would reject being assimilated to Jagannātha worship.

descriptions: Nine unconditioned dharmas, including the suchness of good, bad and neutral dharmas, of the path and of dependent origination (Vasumitra; low confidence).
negations: Past and future do not exist (Vasumitra).
views.relation_to_self: No self (general Sthavira position).
views.relation_to_world: Only the present and the unconditioned exist.
views.caveat: Reconstructed from doxography; the 'suchness' dharmas are unconditioned categories, not a single ground.

descriptions: The Lord who reveals all scripture through five faces, as five streams (Kāmika pūrva 1.20–27).
Śiva's knowledge (śivajñāna) is the higher knowledge revealing the Lord; lower knowledges reveal the bound soul and its bonds (Kāmika pūrva 1.14–17).
In the Kashmirian reading, the Lord's teaching is one, graded as difference (Śiva tantras), difference-in-identity (Rudra tantras) and non-difference (Bhairava tantras) (Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18).
views.relation_to_self: Disputed within the Mantramārga: the Siddhānta holds the soul eternally distinct, becoming equal to Śiva in liberation; the Bhairava-tantra exegetes of Kashmir hold identity.
views.relation_to_world: The Lord acts on the world through his power(s) and mantras; the Siddhānta treats māyā as a real material cause distinct from Śiva, the non-dual exegetes as Śiva's self-manifestation.
views.caveat: The Mantramārga is not doctrinally uniform. The Saiddhāntikas reject the non-dual reading of their scriptures and the identity of soul and Śiva; a one-truth reading must record this denial.

descriptions: Svacchandabhairava, a form of Aghora/Bhairava, worshipped with his consort Aghoreśvarī.
views.caveat: Known here only at catalogue level; the Svacchandatantra's own doctrine is recorded by U19.

names.name: Śabda-brahman = the consciousness of all beings

descriptions: the supreme Lord, splendid with being, consciousness and bliss, with parts (sakala), from whom Śakti, nāda and bindu arise (ŚT 1.7)
śabda-brahman is the consciousness of all beings (ŚT 1.13)
negations: śabda-brahman is neither the word nor its meaning, both of which are insentient (ŚT 1.12–13)
views.relation_to_self: The same consciousness dwells in each body as kuṇḍalinī and becomes the letters (ŚT 1.14).
views.relation_to_world: The world of words and of things unfolds from the supreme through Śakti, nāda, bindu and the fifty letters (ŚT 1.7–16).
views.caveat: The mantra manuals serve worshippers of many deities (Śiva, Viṣṇu, the Goddess, Gaṇeśa, Sūrya) and adopt a Śaiva–Śākta cosmogony of sound; they are not a separate darśana and would defer to the metaphysics of the worshipper's own school.

names.name: svasambodha (one's own awareness), unbounded and complete

descriptions: one's own awareness, unbounded (nirmaryāda) and complete (sampūrṇa) - the Mata line quoted at TĀ 4.263a
the undivided (akhaṇḍa) supreme reality (TĀ 4.269-270)
views.relation_to_self: The ultimate is one's own awareness.
views.relation_to_world: Not recorded.
views.caveat: Reconstructed only from the Trika exegetes' reports (Abhinavagupta, Jayaratha); the Mata's own texts are not identified here, so this view is provisional.

names.name: niḥśreyasa (the highest good to which dharma joins a person)

descriptions: Dharma is the beneficial object (artha) whose mark is Vedic injunction (MS 1.1.2).
Injunction alone can make known what is past, present, future, subtle, hidden or remote; no sense faculty can (Śabara on MS 1.1.2).
The Veda is authorless and eternal, its word-meaning relation original, and it is therefore a self-sufficient means of knowing dharma (MS 1.1.5, 1.1.27–32).
negations: No creator who composes the Veda or dispenses the fruits of action is established (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 42–116; Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 7).
Deities are not the principal element of a rite, nor embodied eaters of offerings (MS 9.1.9 with Śabara).
No person perceives dharma directly (ŚV codanā 110–136).
views.relation_to_self: Selves are many, eternal and all-pervading; each is agent and enjoyer of the fruits of its own ritual action.
views.relation_to_world: The world is real and beginningless, with no total creation or dissolution; it is the field in which dharma and adharma ripen.
views.caveat: Classical Mīmāṃsā posits no single ultimate in the Vedāntic sense: no Brahman as the one ground of all and no creator Īśvara. Its highest authority is the authorless Veda, its highest object dharma, whose declared fruit is heaven (svarga) and, for later teachers, release as the end of embodiment. Reading dharma or the Veda as a name of 'the One' of RV 1.164.46 is an interpretation the classical school does not make. Later theistic Mīmāṃsakas (Āpadeva, Laugākṣi Bhāskara, Vedānta Deśika) dedicate dharma to Govinda/Īśvara, but still do not make the Lord the subject matter of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā.

descriptions: the dark one wearing the peacock crown, her husband
the physician of love's wound
views.relation_to_self: The soul is his bride and servant.
views.relation_to_world: Family honour and the world's shame are to be cast off for him.
views.caveat: A song-tradition without a formal theology; songs using the name ('Rām ratan') are read by some as nirguṇa, by most as devotion to Kṛṣṇa.

descriptions: the cessation of the round of dependent origination, reached by seeing the arising and passing of consciousness and feeling
views.caveat: Low confidence; no primary text read.

descriptions: Doctrinally follows the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma of the Kośa: nirvāṇa as cessation through discernment.
negations: No self (AK 3.18).
views.relation_to_self: As in the Sarvāstivāda.
views.relation_to_world: As in the Sarvāstivāda.
views.caveat: The Mūlasarvāstivāda is known chiefly as a Vinaya lineage; in Tibet its monks hold Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna views of the ultimate, which belong to other lineages' entries.

descriptions: Shares the general Mīmāṃsā orientation to dharma known from the Veda; its distinctive surviving teaching concerns only how the validity of cognition is known.
views.caveat: Almost nothing of this school's metaphysics survives; this view is a minimal placeholder inherited from the parent school and should not be read as a reconstructed doctrine.

names.name: the Jina (worshipped in his image, sthāpanā-jina)

descriptions: the liberated Jina, present to the worshipper through the consecrated image as a support for recalling his qualities
the model of the worshipper's own purified self
negations: the Jina does not receive offerings or grant favours
the image is not itself divine apart from what it represents
views.relation_to_self: Worship of the Jina's qualities purifies the worshipper toward the same state.
views.relation_to_world: Real and uncreated; the images and temples are supports within it.
views.caveat: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator: liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct, and the universe of six substances is uncreated. It can accept 'one truth, many names' only in its own way — as many-sidedness (anekānta) about a plural reality — not as the identity of all souls in one substance. Image worship here is devotion to the qualities of a liberated soul, not to a creator-god.

descriptions: Knowledge alone is: knower, knowing and known are one aṟivu (Ātmopadeśa Śatakam).
views.relation_to_self: The Self is that knowledge; the one God of all humans.
views.relation_to_world: The world is superimposed on the one reality (Darśana Mālā, adhyāropa and apavāda).
views.caveat: His social teaching (one caste, one religion) is an ethical corollary of non-duality, not a separate doctrine.

descriptions: stainless, motionless, eternal, actionless, attributeless, great, sky-like knowledge and bliss (GŚ 99)
the samarasa of body and supreme state (SSP 5)
the state where the mind sees the mind in sahaja-samādhi (AmŚ 54)
negations: fearless, supportless, without elaboration, without resting-place, formless (GŚ 92)
neither temple nor mosque (Gorakh Bānī)
views.relation_to_self: The self is Śiva; the yogī enters the supreme 'like milk into milk' and becomes non-dual (GŚ 100); the guru's grace unites body and pada.
views.relation_to_world: The whole cosmos is within the body (piṇḍa-brahmāṇḍa); the body is to be perfected, not merely transcended.
views.caveat: The Nāth texts affirm one supreme under many names and place all schools beneath it, but they insist that it is reached through the body and the guru, not through scripture or reasoning; a one-truth reading that ignores the body-centred path would misstate them.

descriptions: The one omniscient supreme self; His cognition, desire and effort are eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).
His convention 'from this word this meaning is to be understood' is the denotative power of words; all Vedic statements are valid because He spoke them (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Proved as the maker of earth, sprouts and the like because they are effects (Gaṅgeśa; Viśvanātha).
Viśvanātha salutes Kṛṣṇa as the seed of the tree of saṃsāra (Bhāṣāpariccheda 1).
negations: not the material cause of the world
no non-eternal cognition (His cognition is eternal)
views.relation_to_self: The supreme self is one of the two kinds of self; individual selves are distinct in each body, all-pervading and eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).
views.relation_to_world: Maker (efficient cause) of all effects; the categories are real and exactly definable.
views.caveat: As for Nyāya; in addition, Navya-Nyāya's analysis never admits a featureless or indeterminable ultimate, and it defends the exact definability of categories against Advaita's claim that they are indeterminable.

names.name: the Lord of each shrine (Tillaiyampalavāṇaṉ, Ārūraṉ …)

descriptions: love itself (Tirumantiram 270)
the one whom the Vedas call 'not this, not this', who came as guru and took the devotee as his own
the dancer in the cremation ground and in the golden hall
the thief who stole the heart
negations: beyond the reach of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, who could not find his crown and feet
views.relation_to_self: The devotee is his servant, son or friend; grace melts the heart; love of him is himself.
views.relation_to_world: He dwells in the named temples of the Tamil land; all the universes are motes before him.
views.caveat: Devotional, not scholastic; the hymns praise Śiva as supreme and reject Jain and Buddhist teaching.

descriptions: All is one; God is to be loved and remembered in every being.
views.relation_to_self: Every being is to be seen as God and served.
views.relation_to_world: The world is God's; serve it.
views.caveat: No doctrinal system; devotion to Rāma and Hanumān is central.

descriptions: Holds the parent school's view (ult:sakya).
views.caveat: Shares the Sakya view (see ult:sakya); no separate doctrine of the ultimate is claimed.

descriptions: the stainless formless one
negations: without stain or form
views.relation_to_self: Realized within by yoga and devotion.
views.relation_to_world: The world is his play.
views.caveat: Low-confidence characterization from the sect's name and Rajasthani context.

descriptions: Mind is fundamentally quiescent; 'forgetting feelings' is practice (Zongmi's report).
'The nature of mind is unborn — what need of knowing and seeing?' (Xinming).
negations: 'Originally there is not one dharma — who speaks of cultivation?' (Xinming).
views.caveat: Known mostly through others' reports; the Xinming and Jueguan lun attributions are disputed. Low confidence.

descriptions: The mind is like a bright mirror on its stand, to be wiped constantly (the verse ascribed to Shenxiu, Platform Sūtra 4.6).
views.relation_to_self: The pure mind is one's own, obscured by dust.
views.relation_to_world: Deluded thoughts are adventitious dust.
views.caveat: This is the Northern view as the Platform Sūtra presents it (an opponent's report); Northern texts themselves (Guanxin lun) are only summarised here from memory.

names.name: Śiva (Pinākin) in the invocations of early Naiyāyikas

descriptions: A distinct self (ātmāntara) qualified by virtues: free of demerit, false knowledge and heedlessness; endowed with merit, knowledge and concentration; possessing eightfold lordship (NBh 4.1.21).
He assists human effort and brings about the fruits of action; as a father to his children, so is He to beings (NBh 4.1.21).

The all-knowing, imperishable maker proved from the world's effecthood, the combining of atoms, support and destruction, traditional skills, the validity of the Veda, scripture, the Veda's sentences and special number (NK 5.1).
Reasoning about Him is itself worship; worship of Him is the path to heaven and liberation (NK 1.2–1.3).
The one whom all schools worship under different names — Śiva, Puruṣottama, the Grandfather, the omniscient, the unobstructed … (NK stabaka 1, opening prose).
Author of the Veda, whose validity rests on its being rooted in His perception (Gaṅgeśa).
negations: free of demerit (adharma), false knowledge (mithyājñāna) and heedlessness (pramāda) (NBh 4.1.21)
not the material cause of atoms, selves, ākāśa, time, space or minds, which are eternal
views.relation_to_self: Īśvara is one self among many eternal, all-pervading selves — a special self. Individual selves are eternally distinct from Him and from each other; He makes their karma fruitful. Liberation is not union with Him but the self's absolute release from pain.
views.relation_to_world: Efficient cause of the world: He sets eternal atoms in motion according to the selves' merit and demerit and brings about dissolution; the world of substances, qualities, motions, universals and relations is real, not an appearance.
views.caveat: Nyāya would reject reading 'one truth' as ontological monism: selves are eternally many and distinct from the Lord; atoms, ākāśa, time, space and minds are eternal reals not produced by Him; liberation is not merger. Udayana's statement that all schools worship one Lord under different names is made from within Nyāya theism and does not concede the other schools' doctrines; Buddhists and Mīmāṃsakas named there reject being so included. Nyāya also rejects any levels-of-truth reading of its own realism.

names.name: Samantabhadra (Kun tu bzang po), the dharmakāya primordial buddha
the nature of the sugatas (bde gshegs snying po)
great purity and equality (dag mnyam chen po)

descriptions: All phenomena are primordially buddha: 'from the unborn all is born; in being born there is no birth' (Guhyagarbha ch.2).
Appearances are primordially pure as the maṇḍala of deities (the aggregates are the five buddhas, Guhyagarbha ch.1) and equal in emptiness.
In Mipham's Nyingma reading, buddha-nature is the union of luminosity and emptiness, with the qualities spontaneously present.
negations: no arising, abiding, ceasing, coming or going (Guhyagarbha ch.2)
no bondage and no liberation: 'no one binds, there is no bondage' (Guhyagarbha ch.2)
views.relation_to_self: Beings are primordially buddhas whose own conceptual grasping at 'I' and 'mine' ties 'knots in space'; the 'self' is not established, but the nature of mind is the sugatagarbha.
views.relation_to_world: The world as it appears through karmic delusion is the five realms; as it is, it is the spontaneously present maṇḍala (pure appearance).
views.caveat: The Nyingma deny a creator god and a permanent self: Samantabhadra is the dharmakāya — the ground recognized — not a person who made the world, and the sugatagarbha is not the self of the tīrthikas (Mipham). The one-truth reading is acceptable only as 'one ground, two paths' (recognition and non-recognition), not as the identity of all doctrines.

names.name: Amitābha as one's own mind (yuishin no Mida)

descriptions: The Pure Land is only mind and Amitābha is one's own nature (the Ming Chan–Pure Land formula followed by Ōbaku).
views.relation_to_self: Amitābha recited and the reciter are not two.
views.relation_to_world: The Pure Land is not apart from the purified mind.
views.caveat: Ōbaku holds recitation and Zen to be one; Hakuin's Rinzai criticised this mixture. Low confidence on a specific Ōbaku text stating this.

descriptions: the unconditioned element, object of the path and fruition knowledges, realized after the ultimate realities of mentality-materiality and their causes have been directly seen
views.relation_to_self: only mentality-materiality and their causes are found; no being or self
views.caveat: Follows the Visuddhimagga's account strictly; no ground-of-being reading.

descriptions: Śivādvaita: the non-duality of Śiva taught in agreement with Veda and Vedānta (SSM 3.83–87)
the great liṅga is supreme brahman, the breath the jīva (SSM 12.21–24)
negations: beyond speech and mind, self-luminous, indescribable (SSM 12.21–24)
views.relation_to_self: Difference of Lord and servant governs worship; non-duality is realized at aikya.
views.relation_to_world: The world is Śiva-made, arising from and dissolving into the liṅga.
views.caveat: Would reject any reading that dispenses with worship of the liṅga before realization (SSM 10.37–43).

descriptions: The ṣāḍguṇya — possessor of the six qualities — is the supreme Brahman, cause of all causes, free of all pairs of opposites and all limiting adjuncts (Ahirbudhnya 2.53).
Knowledge is the very form of Brahman; power, lordship, strength, virility and splendour are aspects of that knowledge (Ahirbudhnya 2.56–62).
Śrī/Lakṣmī is his eternal Śakti, inseparable from him, who performs his five acts (Lakṣmī Tantra 12.12–14).
negations: He is called 'without qualities' (nirguṇa) because he is untouched by the qualities of prakṛti (Ahirbudhnya 2.55).
views.relation_to_self: Individual souls depend on Bhagavān; by his grace (śaktipāta) their karmas are equalised and they are lifted from saṃsāra to his presence.
views.relation_to_world: The world issues from his Śakti in a pure creation (the vyūhas) and an other-than-pure creation from prakṛti.
views.caveat: Saṃhitās differ in emphasis (e.g. the Lakṣmī Tantra's Śakti-centred account); Śrīvaiṣṇava readers interpret the Pāñcarātra within qualified non-dualism. The tradition insists on a personal Lord and would reject reading him as an impersonal absolute.

descriptions: Pati: he 'reaches' and 'protects' the paśus by an infinite power of knowledge and by his lordship (PABh on PS 1.1).
Kāraṇa: by will (kāmitva) he produces the whole effect - vidyā, kalā and paśu - all at once or in sequence as he wishes (PABh on PS 2.5-6).
His activity is play (krīḍā): he produces, favours and conceals the threefold effect (PABh on PS 1.9).
Īśāna of all knowledges, lord of all beings, overlord of Brahman, Brahmā; 'may Śiva be mine, always Śiva' (PS 5.42-47, the Īśāna mantra).
Śaṅkara, maker of all happiness and nirvāṇa (PABh on PS 2.20).
negations: he does not depend on karma or on the soul (na karmāpekṣa, PABh on PS 2.6)
he alone is not a paśu (PABh on PS 1.1)
views.relation_to_self: The paśus are all sentient beings other than the Lord, even the gods from Brahmā down and those liberated by Sāṃkhya-Yoga; their bondage is lack of lordship (anaiśvarya). By the rule of practice and the Lord's grace the soul reaches Rudra's proximity (PS 4.19) and union (sāyujya, PS 5.33) and gains his powers of knowing and acting; the Lord alone remains the independent cause.
views.relation_to_world: The effect - the insentient kalās (elements, qualities, organs) and the souls - is eternal yet wholly dependent on the Lord's will; he emits, maintains, withdraws and favours it.
views.caveat: Pāśupata theism keeps the Lord and the soul distinct even in liberation and makes the Lord only the (efficient) cause; it would reject both an impersonal absolute in which the soul dissolves and the Vedāntin claim (BS 2.2.37) that the Lord must also be the material cause.

descriptions: The seer is seeing alone; though pure, it sees by conforming to cognitions (YS 2.20).
Unchanging, it always knows the mind's activities (4.18); consciousness does not move into objects (4.22).
Vyāsa: the power of consciousness is unchanging, does not pass over, has objects shown to it, is pure and infinite (YBh 1.2).
Kaivalya: the guṇas, empty of purpose for the puruṣa, return to their source; or the power of consciousness established in its own form (4.34).
Īśvara: a special puruṣa untouched by afflictions, karma, fruition and residues (1.24), in whom the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed (1.25), teacher of the ancients (1.26), designated by Oṃ (1.27).
negations: not an object (only the seen is object: 4.19)
not the mind, not the buddhi-sattva: 'utterly unmixed' with it (3.35)
not touched by afflictions, karma, fruition or residues (Īśvara, 1.24)
neither the same as buddhi nor wholly different from it (YBh 2.20)
views.relation_to_self: The puruṣa is one's true self (the seer); taking the instrument of seeing for the seer is I-am-ness (2.6) and taking the non-self for the self is ignorance (2.5).
views.relation_to_world: The seen (prakṛti: elements and senses, three guṇas) is real, exists for the sake of the seer — for experience and liberation (2.18, 2.21) — and persists for other puruṣas when it has ceased for one who is liberated (2.22).
views.caveat: Yoga posits many puruṣas (2.22; YBh 2.22), a real prakṛti, and Īśvara as a distinct special puruṣa who is not the material of the world. It does not teach one self of all; a one-truth reading would have to treat this plurality as a standpoint, which Vyāsa and Vācaspati would reject. Vijñānabhikṣu reads Yoga within his Vedānta of non-separation (avibhāga), where souls are non-separate from the Lord — itself a commentator's view. 'Personal or impersonal: both' = the puruṣa is impersonal pure consciousness, Īśvara is personal (a teacher, approached in devotion).

descriptions: The ultimate dimension (nirvāṇa) is not separate from the historical dimension, as water is not separate from waves; it is the extinction of notions such as birth and death, being and non-being.
views.relation_to_self: No separate self; interbeing.
views.relation_to_world: Things inter-are; the world is to be touched deeply in the present moment.
views.caveat: As a Buddhist tradition it does not posit a creator or a substantial absolute; the one-truth reading would be accepted only as 'the ultimate dimension', not as a Self or God.

names.name: kārya / niyoga (what is to be done, known only from the Veda)

descriptions: The Veda's authority lies in making known what is to be done; statements about accomplished things are not independently authoritative (Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 8).
Released, the self remains in mere being (sanmātra), all-pervading, beyond all apprehension (Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 8).
negations: No Īśvara supervises dharma and adharma or creates the world (Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 7, Īśvaranirākaraṇa).
Liberation is not the manifestation of a supreme bliss (Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 8).
Release is not the 'setting' of ignorance (avidyā-astamaya) held by Maṇḍana (Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 8).
views.relation_to_self: Selves are many, eternal and all-pervading; in themselves non-luminous, they appear as subjects in every cognition.
views.relation_to_world: The world is real, arising and perishing in parts, without total creation or dissolution.
views.caveat: The Prābhākaras explicitly deny a supervising Lord and deny that the Veda teaches an existent absolute; any reading of their 'what is to be done' (kārya) as a name of one truth would be foreign to them.

names.name: paramārtha-sat (the ultimately real: the causally efficacious particular)

descriptions: what is capable of causal efficacy is ultimately real (PV 3.3 conventional; NB 1.14–15)
cognition in itself is undivided; grasped and grasper are seen only by distorted vision (PV 3.354 conventional)
the mind is luminous by nature; the stains are adventitious (PV 2.208 conventional)
liberation comes from seeing emptiness (PV 2.253 conventional)
negations: no permanent means of knowledge, no creator God, no eternal self, no authorless Veda (PV Pramāṇasiddhi)
the particular is inexpressible; universals are not real
views.relation_to_self: There is no self; seeing a self is the root of attachment and all faults; seeing selflessness uproots it.
views.relation_to_world: The world of experience consists of momentary particulars; at the higher level it is cognition without real division into subject and object.
views.caveat: The pramāṇa school does not posit a single ultimate being: its 'ultimately real' is a plurality of momentary particulars, and at the cognition-only level non-dual cognition, not a universal consciousness; it explicitly refutes God and any permanent reality. The one-truth reading must record this denial.

descriptions: the nature found by correct seeing, as against the nature found by false seeing, which is conventional truth (MA 6.23)
the reality which is not in the domain of the intellect; the intellect is said to be conventional (BCA 9.2)
the mere negation of own-nature, which implies nothing else in its place (non-implicative negation, prasajya-pratiṣedha)
negations: things arise neither from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without cause (Buddhapālita and Candrakīrti on MMK 1.1; MA 6.8–104)
the self is not found in any of the seven ways the chariot is sought (MA 6.151ff)
no own-nature even conventionally
views.relation_to_self: Both the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of dharmas are emptiness; the view of a real self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the root of saṃsāra and is cut by seeing its object as unfindable (MA 6.120).
views.relation_to_world: The world is not negated as it is known by worldly people; it is accepted by worldly consensus (lokaprasiddhi), without analysis, as conventional truth, while under analysis nothing is found.
views.caveat: The name 'Prāsaṅgika' is a Tibetan classification. Candrakīrti and Śāntideva deny that emptiness is an entity or a thesis to be proved by autonomous inference; any 'one truth' reading as a positive absolute is rejected.

descriptions: consciousness whose essence is reflexive awareness, supreme speech arising of itself; this is the Lord's primary freedom and sovereignty (ĪPK 1.5.13)
throbbing (sphurattā), the great being (mahāsattā), unconditioned by space and time, the Heart of the Supreme (ĪPK 1.5.14)
the knower and doer, already established (ĪPK 1.1.2)
negations: cannot be established or denied by any means of knowledge, since it is the knower itself (ĪPK 1.1.2)
views.relation_to_self: The Lord is one's own self, present but unrecognized, as an unrecognized lover gives no delight (ĪPK 4.17); recognition (pratyabhijñā) reveals it.
views.relation_to_world: Objects are the Lord's manifestations, shown as if separate by his power of māyā while resting within him.
views.caveat: The Pratyabhijñā insists on an enduring conscious subject against the Buddhist denial of self, and on the reality of the Lord's powers of knowing and acting against Vedāntic and grammarian monisms.

descriptions: The unconditioned is the fourth of five knowables; the person, the fifth, is inexpressible (AKBh 9, p. 462).
negations: The person is neither the same as nor different from the aggregates.
The person is neither a real substance nor a mere designation (as the Vātsīputrīyas replied).
views.relation_to_self: They affirm a person (pudgala) but not the self (ātman) of the outsiders; its relation to the aggregates and to nirvāṇa is inexpressible.
views.relation_to_world: The person transmigrates, bearing the aggregates, until its cessation in nirvāṇa (low confidence).
views.caveat: Known mainly through opponents; the Pudgalavādins insisted their person was not the ātman of other schools, and would reject assimilation to it.

descriptions: The supreme truth from which the world's birth, maintenance and end proceed, self-luminous, free of deception (BhP 1.1.1).
One non-dual reality called Brahman, Paramātman and Bhagavān (BhP 1.2.11); Bhagavān has the six excellences (VP 6.5.74-79).
The world is the śakti of the supreme Brahman, like the spreading light of a fire (VP 1.22.56); Viṣṇu's śakti is threefold (VP 6.7.61).
One Lord takes the names Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva by function (VP 1.2.66).
Śiva alone is both partless Brahman and with form, worshipped in the liṅga (ŚiP 1.5.10-13); the unmarked is the root of the mark (LiP 1.3.1).
The Goddess is eternal, the world is her form; she alone exists and her powers return into her (DM 1; 10).
negations: the Lord's gross and subtle forms negated as superimposed by ignorance, for the vision of Brahman (BhP 1.3.30-33)
the supreme reality cannot be spoken, beyond words (VP 6.7.100)
Brahman beyond sat and asat before creation (BhP 2.9.32)
views.relation_to_self: Varies by text: non-difference once ignorance is gone (VP 6.7.93-96; BhP 12.5.11) alongside the devotee's eternal service that refuses even oneness (BhP 3.29.13); the self is 'made of nirvāṇa and knowledge' (VP 6.7.22).
views.relation_to_world: The world is the Lord's power and play (līlā), manifested and withdrawn in cycles of creation and dissolution; the Lord pervades beings as the elements pervade things, 'in them and not in them' (BhP 2.9.34).
views.caveat: The Purāṇas are not one school: Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva and Śākta Purāṇas each name their deity as the ultimate and often subordinate the others; passages of identity (VP 1.2.66; the Kūrma) coexist with sectarian ranking. Commentators read the same Purāṇa as non-dual (Śrīdhara) or as teaching eternal difference (Madhva) or inconceivable difference-in-identity (Jīva). A 'one truth' reading is supported by some passages and rejected by sectarian commentators.

names.name: Sukhāvatī, the Pure Land of Peace and Bliss (Anle, Anyang, Jile)
the uncreated dharma-body of true wisdom (zhenshi zhihui wuwei fashen)

descriptions: The three adornments of the land, the Buddha and the bodhisattvas 'enter the one dharma-phrase': the pure phrase, which is the uncreated dharma-body of true wisdom (Rebirth Treatise, T1524 232b22-25).
The Pure Land surpasses the paths of the three realms, is ultimately like space, vast and boundless (T1524 230c21-22); it is not included in the three realms (Tanluan, Daochuo).
Amitābha now present is a reward-body buddha and his land a reward land (Daochuo, Anle ji 5c; Shandao).
The dharma-body of dharma-nature gives rise to the dharma-body of expedient means and the latter manifests the former; different but inseparable, one but not identical (Tanluan's Commentary).
negations: Birth there is 'the birth of non-birth', not the deluded birth of the three existences (T1958 11c11-14).
The Buddha seen in samādhi neither comes nor goes; mind makes the buddha (Pratyutpanna; Contemplation Sūtra 8).
views.relation_to_self: Beings are ordinary foolish beings bound by passions (fanfu) who cannot reach awakening by their own power in this age; they are embraced by the Buddha's light and vow; in the Chan-inflected reading, 'this mind is the Buddha' and Amitābha is the Buddha of one's own nature, but birth in the West is still to be sought.
views.relation_to_world: This Sahā world of five turbidities is to be loathed and left; Sukhāvatī, created by Dharmākara's vows, lies west beyond ten trillion buddha-lands; for the mind-only reading the pure land is where the mind is pure, without denying the Western land.
views.caveat: Pure Land teachers insist on the distinctness of Amitābha and his land from the practitioner ('pointing to a direction and establishing form') and would reject a reading that dissolves the Western land into a symbol of one truth; they accept the Mahāyāna identity of all buddhas in dharma-nature but hold that one must rely on this Buddha's vow. The equation of Amitābha with a single ultimate is therefore made only in the interpretation layer and only under P1-level.

descriptions: Being-consciousness-bliss (sat-cit-ānanda), pure (śuddha) — untouched by māyā.
The locus of contradictory attributes (viruddha-dharmāśraya): with and without qualities, moving and unmoving.
Puruṣottama is the highest; Akṣara Brahman is his abode and the goal of knowers; Antaryāmin dwells within.
Madhurāṣṭaka: everything of the lord of sweetness is sweet.
negations: Denies that māyā has any part in Brahman or in the world's reality (against Śaṅkara's māyāvāda).
views.relation_to_self: The soul is a spark-like part (aṃśa) of Brahman in which bliss (ānanda) is concealed by the Lord's will; by grace it is manifested in service.
views.relation_to_world: The world is Brahman itself, transformed without change (avikṛta-pariṇāma); real and to be honoured; only saṃsāra — the soul's 'I and mine' — is unreal.
views.caveat: The impersonal Akṣara is held lower than Puruṣottama; Puṣṭimārga would reject any equalising of the knower's Brahman and the devotee's Kṛṣṇa.

descriptions: the Lord of love, source of the Shabd
negations: beyond all names
views.relation_to_self: As in Sant Mat.
views.relation_to_world: As in Sant Mat.
views.caveat: As in Sant Mat.

descriptions: the true name revealed by Soamiji
negations: beyond all lower regions
views.relation_to_self: The surat is its drop.
views.relation_to_world: As in Sant Mat.
views.caveat: The Agra lines hold that the name itself was newly revealed by Soamiji; other Sant Mat lines treat it differently.

descriptions: love (hita) itself, appearing as the pair in eternal play
Rādhā, whose favour even Madhusūdana seeks
negations: no separation, birth-story or departure in the eternal play
views.relation_to_self: The soul's true identity is as a sakhī who delights in the pair's joy.
views.relation_to_world: The world is not the focus; the eternal Vṛndāvana is the reality contemplated.
views.caveat: The tradition rejects making Rādhā a power of Kṛṣṇa or reducing the pair's love to an impersonal absolute; love, not Brahman, is its first term.

descriptions: The Rāghavendra Maṭha holds the Dvaita teaching on the ultimate without variation; see ult:dvaita.
views.relation_to_self: As in ult:dvaita.
views.relation_to_world: As in ult:dvaita.
views.caveat: As in ult:dvaita; the maṭha has no separate doctrine of the ultimate.

descriptions: Brahman and Śakti are one, like fire and its power to burn; at rest it is called Brahman, in creating, preserving and destroying it is called Śakti.
God is with form and without form, and beyond both; the vijñānī sees that Brahman has become the universe and its beings.
Vivekananda: each soul is potentially divine.
negations: Brahman cannot be described: the salt doll that went to measure the ocean dissolved in it
views.relation_to_self: The Self is Brahman; the individual is Śiva (jīva is Śiva), so service to beings is worship.
views.relation_to_world: The world is the Mother's play (līlā); to the jñānī it is māyā, to the vijñānī it is Brahman itself.
views.caveat: The order would reject a reading that ranks form below formless: Ramakrishna held both true. It welcomes the one-truth reading ('as many faiths, so many paths').

descriptions: Existence-consciousness-bliss, the one Self that shines as 'I-I' when the ego subsides.
The Heart is the Self, the source from which the I-thought rises.
negations: not the body, the senses, the vital breath, the mind or the ignorance of sleep (Nāṉ Yār)
views.relation_to_self: Identical: the Self is what one truly is; the ego is a false knot of consciousness and the body.
views.relation_to_world: The world appears when the mind rises and disappears in deep sleep; it has no reality apart from the Self. Taught by level: for beginners creation is admitted; the final truth is non-origination.
views.caveat: Ramana also spoke of God and guru as the Self and worshipped Arunachala as Śiva; the tradition would reject treating his teaching as mere philosophy apart from silence and grace.

descriptions: the supreme Brahman who, formless, becomes embodied through the devotee's love (Mānas 1.116)
the master in the form of all moving and unmoving beings (Mānas 4.3)
whose name is greater than both his forms (Mānas 1.18–28)
negations: without qualities, without form, unseen, unborn (Mānas 1.116)
views.relation_to_self: The soul is Rāma's servant; the exclusive devotee holds 'I am the servant' unwaveringly.
views.relation_to_world: The world is full of Sītā and Rāma and to be bowed to; seen through māyā ('I and mine') it binds, and is like a dream beside worship of Hari.
views.caveat: The tradition would reject any reading that makes the embodied Rāma lower than the formless; the name is held greater than both.

descriptions: Rāma, reached by the path of devotion
the formless Brahman beyond the elements, known by discrimination
negations: not the elements, not the body
views.relation_to_self: The Self beyond body and elements is Brahman; the accomplished abide in it.
views.relation_to_world: The world is to be lived in with effort and vigilance while knowing the Self.
views.caveat: Devotion to Rāma and Advaita discrimination are held together; neither is dropped.

descriptions: the nirguṇa Rām loved by his 'lovers'
negations: without image
views.relation_to_self: Remembered within.
views.relation_to_world: Pervades all.
views.caveat: Low-confidence characterization.

names.name: the conscious light (cinmaya jyotis), supreme bliss

descriptions: Liberation in life is knowledge of identity with Śiva in an ageless, deathless body (Rasārṇava 1.8).

The conscious light between the brows: supreme bliss, of the nature of light, free of conception, peaceful, self-known; seeing the whole world as consciousness one attains brahmanhood here (Rasahṛdaya 1.21-23; SDS 46-48).
Mercury is Śiva's own seed and is praised as equal to the supreme brahman (Rasārṇava 1.36; SDS 49-51).
negations: Free of conception (avikalpa), free of all afflictions (Rasahṛdaya 1.22).
views.relation_to_self: The Raseśvaras are Māheśvaras who hold identity (tādātmya) with the Supreme Lord; the self realizes it only in a stable body.
views.relation_to_world: The world is to be seen as consciousness; mercury and mica, seeds of Śiva and the Goddess, make the divine body.
views.caveat: The tradition would reject any one-truth reading that allows liberation without the stable, undecaying body ('liberation after the body falls is meaningless'). Its practices are restricted and are recorded here only in summary.

descriptions: sandalwood to the devotee's water
the Lord of the poor who raises the lowly
the king of Begampura
negations: no difference between you and me in truth
views.relation_to_self: As gold and bracelet, water and wave.
views.relation_to_world: Begampura: a world without grief, tax, fear or rank is the Lord's city.
views.caveat: The modern Ravidassia Dharam distinguishes itself from Sikh readings of the same hymns; recorded as context.

descriptions: you alone, Śrī Hari, appear in endless forms (Narsinh)
Brahman is one for king and servant (Annamācārya)
views.relation_to_self: Varies by poet; Narsinh: until the Self is known all practice is false.
views.relation_to_world: Varies by poet.
views.caveat: Not a tradition: a classificatory grouping; each poet's view should be read with the tradition that claims him.

names.name: the Great Madhyamaka (dbu ma chen po), in Kongtrul's presentation
the unity of appearance and emptiness; primordial purity (Mipham)
the single intent (dgongs pa gcig) of the lineages' final views — Dzogchen, Mahāmudrā, Lamdre, the Great Madhyamaka

descriptions: each of the eight practice lineages is a complete path to the same buddhahood
buddha-nature as the union of luminosity and emptiness (Mipham)
the other-empty Great Madhyamaka as the view for meditation, the self-empty Madhyamaka for cutting elaborations in study (Kongtrul, as recalled)
negations: no single school's formulation is the only valid one
the ultimate is neither a mere absence nor a permanent entity (Mipham)
views.relation_to_self: As in the lineages it preserves: buddha-nature present in all beings; the imputed self does not exist.
views.relation_to_world: As in the lineages it preserves.
views.caveat: Rimé is an approach, not a doctrine: its masters insisted that each lineage keep its own view and methods unmixed, and they themselves differed (Kongtrul's shentong-leaning Great Madhyamaka; Mipham's Madhyamaka of unity). Reading it as a single 'one-truth' doctrine would erase the distinctions it insists on. Gelug critics rejected parts of the Rimé masters' views (see dsp:mipham-gelug-madhyamaka).

names.name: the true person of no rank

descriptions: Seen directly in kenshō when the great doubt shatters (Hakuin).
'Beings are originally buddhas, like water and ice' (Zazen wasan).
negations: No-thought; beyond being and non-being (Wumenguan case 1 commentary).
views.relation_to_self: The seeing nature is one's own; 'this very place is the Lotus Land, this very body the Buddha' (Zazen wasan closing).
views.relation_to_world: The world seen after kenshō is the Pure Land here; compassion flows as the 'four wisdoms'.
views.caveat: Rinzai insists the nature must be seen, not merely believed; it criticises the view that sitting in quiet is itself awakening ('dead sitting').

descriptions: the Word heard as sound and seen as light, in all scriptures
negations: not the spoken name
views.relation_to_self: The soul is of the same essence.
views.relation_to_world: The Word creates and sustains all.
views.caveat: Presented as the common core of all religions — a claim the religions named do not themselves make.

descriptions: An all-pervading divine power felt as a cool breeze after realization (claims of the tradition).
views.relation_to_self: Self-realization is the union of individual attention with the spirit via kuṇḍalinī.
views.relation_to_world: The world is sustained by the divine power.
views.caveat: The tradition identifies its founder with the Ādi Śakti; a one-truth reading would not be accepted if it denied that claim.

descriptions: merciful to the poor
views.relation_to_self: Found in the human.
views.relation_to_world: Hindu and Muslim equal.
views.caveat: Low-confidence characterization from ethnographic reports.

descriptions: one, eternally free (anādimukta), omniscient and omnipotent
a mass of consciousness, pervasive, ever-risen, tranquil, who favours all (Tattvaprakāśa 1)
acts by a single conscious power (śakti) and has no body of māyā; for worship, a body of mantras
performs the five acts for the souls' release
negations: not the material cause of the world
not identical with souls
unchanged by his acts
views.relation_to_self: Souls are eternal and many, distinct from Śiva; freed, each becomes equal to Śiva (a 'Śiva') in knowledge and agency without becoming him.
views.relation_to_world: The world is real, produced from māyā (and bindu) as material cause, with Śiva as efficient cause; it exists to ripen and release souls.
views.caveat: Accepts one supreme Lord but denies that souls and māyā are his appearances; a 'one truth' reading that collapses souls or the world into Śiva is rejected.

descriptions: Before creation the Goddess alone existed; she produced the cosmic egg and the gods (Bahvṛca Upaniṣad; Devī Gītā 7.32).
She is eternal and the world is her form; yet for the gods' sake she is born again and again (Devī Māhātmya 1).
She abides in all beings as consciousness, intelligence, sleep, hunger, power, faith, peace, compassion and mother (Devī Māhātmya 5).
She is Mahāmāyā, who drags even the minds of the wise into delusion, and when pleased grants liberation (Devī Māhātmya 1).
She declares herself Brahman, of the nature of consciousness (Devī Upaniṣad).
negations: nirguṇā, niṣkalā, nirākārā — without qualities, parts or form (Lalitā Sahasranāma 43-45)
beyond the three gods' consorts, 'a certain fourth', hard to reach, of boundless greatness (Saundaryalaharī 98)
views.relation_to_self: She alone is the self and what is other than her is unreal (Bahvṛca 5); she abides in beings as consciousness (Devī Māhātmya 5).
views.relation_to_world: The world is her manifestation and her body; she creates, sustains and withdraws it and deludes and liberates through her power of māyā.
views.caveat: Śāktas name the ultimate as the feminine Śakti, the Mother, and many resist readings that make her a mere attribute of a male god or that make the world she manifests unreal; but Śākta texts themselves identify her with the Brahman of the Upaniṣads and declare all goddesses her forms, which fits the one-truth reading.

names.name: 'khor 'das dbyer med — the inseparability of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa
kun gzhi rgyu rgyud — the all-base causal continuum
gsal stong zung 'jug — the union of clarity and emptiness
Mahāmudrā, the result continuum (phyag rgya chen po 'bras bu'i rgyud)
spros bral — freedom from elaborations (Madhyamaka, as in Gorampa)

descriptions: The all-base (ālaya) as causal continuum holds saṃsāra and nirvāṇa both (Vajra Verses, Derge 139b.1).
The result is Mahāmudrā, the result continuum, known through the four result-empowerments as omniscience (Vajra Verses 139b.2–3).
Pure vision: the inexhaustible ornamental wheel of the Sugatas' body, speech and mind (Vajra Verses 139a.7).
The ultimate is free from the four extremes of existence, non-existence, both and neither (Gorampa, Distinguishing the Views).
negations: not merely the absence of inherent existence (Gorampa, against Tsongkhapa)
not an other-empty permanent entity (Gorampa, against Dolpopa)
'If grasping arises, it is not the view' (Parting from the Four Attachments, line 4)
views.relation_to_self: The individual mind-stream as ālaya is the causal continuum in which the result is present as potential; realizing its clarity-emptiness frees it from the self-grasping of the impure vision.
views.relation_to_world: The three visions: the world as seen by beings with afflictions (impure), by yogins in meditation (experiential), and by buddhas (pure) — one reality appearing according to the purity of mind.
views.caveat: Sakya teachers would reject any reading of 'inseparability of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa' as a substantial one-reality behind appearances; Gorampa's freedom from elaboration denies even that emptiness is an entity. The Lamdre view is realized through empowerment and the two stages, not by reasoning alone.

descriptions: Śiva and Śakti are equal in primacy, sharing a fivefold equality of seat, state, action, form and name (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 41).
The Goddess worshipped in the thousand-petalled lotus, where the Śrīcakra is the moon-disc (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 10).
views.relation_to_self: The Goddess is realized within, in the space of the heart and the crown; the Samayin identifies the cakra with his own inner space.
views.relation_to_world: The world is produced by the Śiva-Śakti pair acting together as father and mother (SL 41).
views.caveat: The Samaya school rejects the uttara-Kaula view that only the Śakti principle exists and the pūrva-Kaula view that makes Śiva her body alone; any reconciliation with Kaula views must record this objection.

descriptions: Puruṣa: conscious, witness, isolated, neutral, seer, non-agent; neither a producer nor a product; many (SK 3, 11, 17–19).

Prakṛti (mūlaprakṛti, pradhāna, the unmanifest): unconscious, one and common, made of the three guṇas, uncaused, the productive root of all the manifest; inferred from its effects (SK 3, 8, 10–11, 15–16).
Everything other than prakṛti and puruṣa is impermanent (SS 5.72).
negations: Puruṣa is neither prakṛti nor vikṛti — neither a producer nor a product (SK 3).
No one (no puruṣa) is bound, released or transmigrates; prakṛti is (SK 62).
The liberating knowledge: 'I am not, (nothing is) mine, not I' (SK 64).
Liberation is not the manifestation of bliss, since puruṣa has no properties (SS 5.74).
views.relation_to_self: The self is puruṣa: each person is a distinct puruṣa, pure consciousness mistakenly identified with buddhi and the instruments; liberation is the isolation (kaivalya) of that consciousness.
views.relation_to_world: The world is the real transformation (pariṇāma) of prakṛti, pre-existing in it (satkārya), which acts for the experience and liberation of puruṣas and ceases for the puruṣa who has discriminated (SK 21, 56–59, 65–66).
views.caveat: Classical Sāṃkhya posits two irreducible kinds of ultimate — the many puruṣas and the one prakṛti — and would reject reading them as aspects or parts of a single ultimate; it recognizes no established Īśvara (SS 1.92) and reads scriptural statements of non-duality as sameness of kind among puruṣas (SS 1.154). 'Impersonal' here means there is no personal Lord; puruṣa (literally 'person') is attributeless consciousness. Theistic forms of Sāṃkhya (the epic 'twenty-sixth principle', Vijñānabhikṣu) add a Lord.

names.name: Brahman, consciousness-bliss, called Īśvara and liṅga (ŚR 1.2.4)

descriptions: the consciousness of all beings, unfolded as the world; bliss, without a second (ŚR 1.3.1)
Brahman is consciousness-bliss, self-luminous, stainless, called Īśvara and liṅga, unborn, all-pervading, changeless, formless, all-powerful and omniscient (ŚR 1.2.4–5)
Brahmā, Janārdana, the supreme Śakti and Maheśvara are forms of nāda (Bṛhaddeśī 17–18)
negations: changeless (nirvikāra) and formless (nirākāra) (ŚR 1.2.5)
views.relation_to_self: The jīvas are parts of Brahman, like sparks of fire, conditioned by beginningless avidyā and bound by karma; they are not different from the self (ŚR 1.2.5–6, 1.2.11).
views.relation_to_world: Brahman creates the world by its power as gold becomes earrings — or, 'others say', through avidyā as a rope appears as a snake; Śārṅgadeva reports both views (ŚR 1.2.11–12).
views.caveat: The music treatises borrow their metaphysics (Vedāntic and Śaiva) and record rival views of creation without deciding them; 'nāda-brahman' names the ultimate as approached through sound, not a separate doctrine of the ultimate.

descriptions: The Self realized by the renouncer as 'so'ham' — 'I am He' (Maitreya 2.1; Nāradaparivrājaka 9).
The sixteenth measure of the praṇava and the state beyond the fourth (Nāradaparivrājaka 8; Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka).
That in which renunciation consists: the union of jīva and the supreme (Maitreya 2.17).
negations: neti neti (Nāradaparivrājaka 9, quoting the Bṛhadāraṇyaka)
not reached by staff, shaving, garb or show (Nāradaparivrājaka 5)
views.relation_to_self: Identical: the renouncer's own Self is Brahman, and the jīva in the body-temple is Śiva alone (Maitreya 2.1; Avadhūta 1). In the Vaiṣṇava Śāṭyāyanīya the renouncer serves Viṣṇu and bears his marks.
views.relation_to_world: The world is renounced as the field of the three desires (for wife, wealth and worlds); for the knower it is superimposed and no longer binding; rites cease because 'the sun of consciousness neither rises nor sets' (Maitreya 2.14).
views.caveat: The renunciate ideal is a way of life before it is a doctrine: the texts insist that the ultimate is realized only by one who has actually abandoned the ritual world, and they disagree among themselves (Advaitin paramahaṃsa vs Vaiṣṇava tridaṇḍin) on whether outer marks are to be kept. A one-truth reading must not dissolve that insistence on renunciation or the Vaiṣṇava strand's theism.

checks.note: The cited passages are located: Maitreya 2.1 (deho devālayaḥ … so'haṃbhāvena), 2.14 (the sun of consciousness), 2.17; Nāradaparivrājaka 8 (the sixteen-measured praṇava), 9 (brahmasvarūpa, neti neti) and 5 (not by staff or garb). 'Avadhūta 1' is cited for 'the jīva is Śiva', but Avadhūta 1 is the etymology of 'avadhūta'. The Śiva identity is in Maitreya 2.1 and Skanda 6-10.

descriptions: in every body, 'in the breath of the breath'
the one of Hindu and Turk
the Beloved whose redness colours the lover
known in sahaj, beyond the three qualities
negations: neither one nor two (Kabīr)
not in temple, mosque, Kaaba or Kailāsa
not the son of Daśaratha
without form or sign
views.relation_to_self: The Lord dwells within the self as musk in the deer; when the 'I' goes, Hari is; like gold and bracelet, water and wave (Ravidās).
views.relation_to_world: The world is māyā's play and Kāl's grinding-mill, yet the Lord pervades it; Hindu and Turk, caste and sect are human constructions.
views.caveat: The Sants would reject any reading that makes their Rām an avatāra or an image, or that reduces their Beloved to an impersonal abstraction; they also resist being enrolled in any scriptural system, Hindu or Muslim.

descriptions: the ocean of consciousness and love from which the sound current flows
reached beyond Sach Khand
negations: nameless (Anāmī)
beyond Brahm, the god of the Vedas
beyond mind and matter
views.relation_to_self: The soul (surat) is a drop of that ocean; it returns and merges while retaining (on most accounts) the bliss of love.
views.relation_to_world: The lower creation is Kāl's domain; the Supreme's mercy (Dayāl) acts through the Saints.
views.caveat: Sant Mat ranks other traditions' ultimates (Brahm, Nirañjan, Pārbrahm) as lower regions — a hierarchy that those traditions do not accept.

descriptions: reached through light and sound to the soundless
negations: beyond sound
views.relation_to_self: The self realizes itself in the soundless.
views.relation_to_world: All scriptures point to it.
views.caveat: Low-confidence characterization.

descriptions: the one god, lord of the meeting rivers (Basava)
the beautiful one without death, decay or form (Akka Mahādēvi)
the void in which liṅga and aṅga are not two (Allama)
negations: not the many gods of pot and winnowing fan (Basava)
bayalu — no enclosure (Allama)
views.relation_to_self: The devotee is servant (dāsōhaṃ), bride and finally one with the liṅga.
views.relation_to_world: The world is to be lived in through work as worship and sharing; the moving devotee is Śiva's temple.
views.caveat: Many in this strand reject framing the vacanas' Lord in Vedāntic or Sanskrit-philosophical terms.

descriptions: Cessation through discernment: disjunction from all sāsrava dharmas, a real (dravya), unconditioned, eternal dharma, obtained separately for each bond (AK 1.5–6).
One of the three objects of refuge, with the Buddha's and the Saṅgha's pure dharmas (AK 4.32).
negations: There is no self; only aggregates conditioned by defilement and karma (AK 3.18).
Things do not arise from Īśvara or any single cause (AK 2.64).
views.relation_to_self: No self exists; nirvāṇa is not the attainment of a self but the cessation of the defilements and of future aggregates.
views.relation_to_world: The world of conditioned dharmas is real in all three times; nirvāṇa is a real unconditioned dharma alongside it, not its ground.
views.caveat: The Sarvāstivāda recognizes many ultimately real dharmas (paramārthasat) and three unconditioned ones; it would reject reading nirvāṇa as a single substance underlying the world or as a self.

descriptions: the divine as the Mother of all, served in the sick and the outcaste
views.relation_to_self: The same Aghora teaching of non-difference, turned toward service.
views.relation_to_world: The world is served, not shunned.
views.caveat: Recent movement; formulation from general reports, not from its own texts.

descriptions: the true name of the formless Lord
negations: no image
views.relation_to_self: The true name within.
views.relation_to_world: All castes equal before him.
views.caveat: Three distinct movements; characterization low confidence.

descriptions: Nirvāṇa is a mere absence: the non-arising of further defilements and births once the antidote has arisen (AKBh 2.55).
negations: No unconditioned is a real entity; space is absence of resistance (AKBh 2.55).
No self as a separate entity; the 'person' is a designation of the series (AKBh 9).
views.relation_to_self: There is no self; clinging to one is the root of all defilements (AKBh 9, p. 461).
views.relation_to_world: Only momentary present dharmas exist; nirvāṇa is their cessation, not a further reality.
views.caveat: The Sautrāntika denies that nirvāṇa is an entity at all; a 'one truth' reading that reifies it is exactly what it argues against.

names.name: empty and calm, numinous awareness (gongjeok yeongji 空寂靈知)

descriptions: The mind that is empty and calm yet numinously aware and never obscured is one's original face and the Dharma-seal transmitted by buddhas and patriarchs (Jinul, Susim kyol).
Samādhi is its substance and prajñā its function; calm and always knowing, knowing and always calm (Susim kyol).
negations: It has no form or characteristic, no size, no boundary, no inside or outside, no birth and death (Susim kyol).
views.relation_to_self: It is the very one who asks the question — the awareness that sees, hears and acts (Susim kyol).
views.relation_to_world: It is not the physical body; the body is 'provisional, arising and ceasing', while 'one thing is ever numinous, covering heaven and earth' (Susim kyol).
views.caveat: Jinul's language of numinous awareness follows Zongmi and the Heze line; Korean critics (Seongcheol) held that this 'understanding-awakening' is not final realization. The tradition would reject reading the true mind as an entity separate from phenomena.

descriptions: Big Mind, including everything; buddha-nature expressed in the posture of zazen.
views.relation_to_self: No separate self; 'I' is a swinging door moved by breath.
views.relation_to_world: Things as it is; practice is enlightenment.
views.caveat: Zen would reject treating 'Big Mind' as a substantial absolute.

names.name: Mahāmudrā of the amulet box (phyag chen ga'u ma)
the four kāyas as self-liberated mind

descriptions: The mind's nature, left uncontrived, is self-liberated; its empty, clear and blissful aspects are the kāyas, 'enclosed together like the two halves of an amulet box' (the tradition's image for the inseparability of ground, path and fruit).
negations: not produced by fabrication
views.relation_to_self: The mind's own nature.
views.relation_to_world: Appearances are carried as the guru, the deity and illusion (the three integrations).
views.caveat: The amulet-box image and the 'three self-liberations' are Shangpa formulations known here only from memory; low confidence.

names.name: the nature of mind, empty and luminous

descriptions: the emptiness whose realization pacifies all suffering
the mind as empty and clear, not to be sought elsewhere
negations: suffering has no ground of its own once its nature is seen
views.relation_to_self: The self is not found; recognizing the mind's nature ends suffering.
views.relation_to_world: The world is impermanent and like a dream; attachment to it is to be abandoned.
views.caveat: Shije is a practice lineage; it does not set out a distinct doctrine of the ultimate beyond the Perfection of Wisdom, and the details of its view survive only in later collections (low confidence).

names.name: Civam (as the source of the medical knowledge)

descriptions: Siddha medicine places itself within the Siddhars' Śaiva frame: Śiva is the first teacher of medicine; body and cosmos share the five elements and the ninety-six principles.
views.relation_to_self: The soul inhabits a body of 96 principles whose health is the balance of the three humours.
views.relation_to_world: The body is built of the five elements, like the world; macrocosm and microcosm correspond.
views.caveat: A medical system: it does not itself argue a doctrine of the ultimate, but borrows the Siddha/Śaiva frame; practitioners hold a range of religious views.

descriptions: God dwells within you as you; the universe is the play of Consciousness (Citi).
views.relation_to_self: The Self is God; the guru's grace awakens this recognition.
views.relation_to_world: The world is the play of Consciousness.
views.caveat: Draws on Kashmir Śaivism; the guru is venerated as the embodiment of grace.

names.name: Paramākāśa / dahara (the supreme ether in the heart)

descriptions: Śiva endowed with cit-śakti, free from all defects, the material and efficient cause of the world.
The supreme ether of the Upaniṣads is his śakti; he is to be meditated on in the small space of the heart.
negations: Denies an attributeless Brahman without śakti.
Denies that Śiva is only the efficient cause.
views.relation_to_self: Souls (paśu) are his body and attribute, distinct yet inseparable; liberated, they become equal to Śiva in bliss (śiva-sāmya) but not identical.
views.relation_to_world: The world is real, a manifestation of the subtle world held in Śiva's śakti.
views.caveat: Appayya Dīkṣita read the school as a step towards Advaita; the school's own text and its Vīraśaiva heirs hold the qualified non-dualism as final.

descriptions: 'Whole being is buddha-nature' (Busshō).
Practice and realization are one: sitting is itself the realization of buddhahood (Bendōwa).
negations: Buddha-nature is not a seed awaiting conditions nor a permanent self; impermanence is buddha-nature (Busshō).
views.relation_to_self: The self forgotten is authenticated by the myriad dharmas (Genjōkōan).
views.relation_to_world: Mountains, waters, time and all beings are the presencing of buddha-nature.
views.caveat: Dōgen rejects the 'Śreṇika heresy' of an eternal mind-nature separate from a perishing body (Bendōwa, Sokushin zebutsu); Sōtō would reject reading buddha-nature as a hidden essence.

names.name: selflessness (bdag med), whose non-realization (ignorance) is the root of all disease
the Medicine Buddha (sangs rgyas sman bla), teacher of the Four Tantras

descriptions: the Four Tantras are taught by the Medicine Buddha's emanation of awareness-wisdom (rig pa'i ye shes)
freedom from ignorance is freedom from the root cause of illness
negations: as long as the self is grasped, the causes of disease follow beings as a bird's shadow follows it
views.relation_to_self: Grasping at a self is the root cause of the three poisons and, through them, of the three nyepa.
views.relation_to_world: The body and its medicines are composed of the five elements; health belongs to the conventional world and serves Dharma, wealth and happiness.
views.caveat: Sowa Rigpa is a science (rig gnas), not a philosophical school; it does not posit its own ultimate and defers to Buddhist teaching (Bön physicians to Bön). This entry records only its framing of health and disease within that teaching.

descriptions: that in which all this rests and from which it has come forth; its nature is unobstructed (Spandakārikā 1.2)
the inner (antarmukha) agency, seat of omniscience, never lost (SK 1.14-16)
the opening and closing of Śaṅkara's eyes (SK 1.1)
negations: where there is neither pain nor pleasure, neither object nor subject, nor even insentience - that exists in the supreme sense (SK 1.5)
views.relation_to_self: It is one's own nature (svabhāva), the knower-agent persisting through all states (SK 1.3, 1.10).
views.relation_to_world: The world emerges and dissolves with the unmeṣa and nimeṣa of the one Śaṅkara (SK 1.1); all particular vibrations rest on the universal vibration (SK 1.19).
views.caveat: Spanda insists that the ultimate is dynamic; it would reject any account of a static, inactive absolute.

descriptions: The movement shares a question rather than an ultimate: what is the visible fruit of the homeless life, and is there fruit of deeds and another world? Each teacher answers differently (DN 2).
negations: Several of its teachers deny any fruit of deeds or any other world (DN 2: Pūraṇa, Ajita).
views.relation_to_self: Contested within the movement: an eternal jīva among seven bodies (Pakudha), a person made of four elements that is annihilated (Ajita), no statement at all (Sañjaya).
views.relation_to_world: Contested: fixed by niyati (Gosāla), eternal and barren (Pakudha), simply ends at death (Ajita).
